articles.title: GXO opens new logistics hub in Malaysia’s Johor-Singapore economic zone
articles.summary: GXO Logistics has opened a new logistics hub in Medini, Malaysia, expanding its operations across the Asia Pacific region. The facility is located within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, a key corridor for regional trade and manufacturing. The new site offers Free Trade Zone benefits and access to major...
articles.body: GXO Logistics has opened a new logistics hub in Medini, Malaysia, expanding its operations across the Asia Pacific region. The facility is located within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, a key corridor for regional trade and manufacturing. The new site offers Free Trade Zone benefits and access to major ports, airports and industrial centres in southern Malaysia and Singapore. Its location allows customers to position inventory closer to regional markets while supporting cross-border supply chains. According to GXO, the facility will serve customers in the technology and advanced industrial sectors. It is already operating as a regional hub for a global supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Supporting regional supply chains The Medini hub forms part of GXO’s expansion strategy in Asia Pacific. The company aims to provide businesses with greater flexibility in managing inventory and distributing goods across regional and international markets. “Asia Pacific continues to be one of the most dynamic growth markets for GXO,” said Michael Jacobs, Chief Executive Officer of the Americas and Asia Pacific at GXO. Jacobs added that the new facility would help customers improve supply chain flexibility and connect with major manufacturing and technology centres. The company is also evaluating additional capabilities for the site, including emerging warehouse technologies. These could improve supply chain visibility and support closer collaboration with customers. However, GXO has not announced a timeline for their introduction. Scott Copeland, Managing Director for Asia Pacific at GXO, highlighted the importance of locating inventory closer to demand. “With access to Singapore and southern Malaysia’s key ports and manufacturing hubs, our new Medini site gives customers a strategic base to scale efficiently and serve both regional and global markets,” said Copeland. The opening strengthens GXO’s regional logistics network as the company continues to develop its operations in Asia Pacific.

The facility is located within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, a key corridor for regional trade and manufacturing.

articles.title: Port of NY/NJ appoints PATH leadership team
articles.summary: The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has announced that PATH Director and General Manager Clarelle DeGraffe will retire at the end of 2026 after more than 37 years with the agency, the last seven leading the PATH rail transit system. James Sincaglia, a long-time NJ Transit executive, has been appointed as...
articles.body: The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has announced that PATH Director and General Manager Clarelle DeGraffe will retire at the end of 2026 after more than 37 years with the agency, the last seven leading the PATH rail transit system. James Sincaglia, a long-time NJ Transit executive, has been appointed as her successor, joined by Matthew Reddell, formerly of Bay Area Rapid Transit in northern California, as deputy director for infrastructure maintenance and rolling stock delivery. Both join Zandra Ford, appointed deputy director for operations in June 2026, completing PATH’s new senior leadership team. DeGraffe will assist in the leadership transition until her retirement. DeGraffe’s tenure as PATH director from March 2019 was marked by transformative achievements. She oversaw the PATH Improvement Plan in 2019 and the PATH Forward programme concluded in March 2026, directed the US$ 2 billion reconstruction of PATH stations, tunnels and equipment devastated by Superstorm Sandy, led the system through the coronavirus pandemic, implemented the tap-to-pay TAPP fare system, oversaw major infrastructure works at Hoboken station and enabled the Every Line Every Day service expansion in spring 2025. Under her leadership in 2022, PATH received the American Public Transportation Association’s Outstanding Public Transportation System Achievement Award for railroads with more than 20 million annual riders. Port Authority Chairman Kevin O’Toole credited DeGraffe for her leadership and mentorship of female staff throughout the agency, noting that PATH has emerged from multiple challenges as a stronger and improved system. DeGraffe described the past seven years as the highlight of her Port Authority career, expressing confidence that the railroad’s leadership is in capable hands as she departs.
takeaways: Both join Zandra Ford, appointed deputy director for operations in June 2026, completing PATH’s new senior leadership team.
DeGraffe will assist in the leadership transition until her retirement.

articles.title: Cisco and PSA Singapore collaborate on AI-driven platform for Tuas Port
articles.summary: Cisco and PSA Singapore have announced a strategic collaboration to develop a proof of concept for an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Port, the world’s largest fully automated container terminal. articles.body: Cisco and PSA Singapore have announced a strategic collaboration to develop a proof of concept for an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Port, the world’s largest fully automated container terminal. The initiative is part of Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration programme, through which Cisco partners with public and private sector organisations to advance national digitalisation priorities and support Singapore’s digital agenda. The platform will unify real-time performance data from PSA’s applications, infrastructure and networking systems into a central view, using AI to map how different services and infrastructure interact. This enables technical teams to quickly identify affected services during an incident, diagnose root causes and receive real-time resolution recommendations. Built-in cloud-native security capabilities protect critical port infrastructure against modern threats, preventing unauthorised access and flagging unusual network activity. The collaboration addresses a pressing operational challenge in modern port environments. Cisco research indicates that the average annual cost of downtime per organisation has reached US$ 300 million, with outages affecting critical systems such as the Terminal Operating System potentially disrupting cargo movement, storage and tracking at scale. The platform is designed to reduce and ultimately pre-empt such unplanned outages. The platform will be implemented first at the Tuas Port Phase 2 Living Lab, providing a real-world environment to test, validate and refine innovations supporting the port’s continued development toward full completion in the 2040s. Nelson Quek, Regional CEO Southeast Asia at PSA International, described digital resilience as fundamental to the reliability and efficiency of global supply chains, framing the Cisco collaboration as reflecting a shared commitment to advancing innovation while reinforcing Singapore’s position as a trusted global trade hub. Bee Kheng Tay, President ASEAN at Cisco, highlighted the need for organisations managing complex critical infrastructure to see, understand and act across their entire technology stack in real time.

articles.body: “Welcome to a Dying Industry” Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Maritime Matters October 29, 2026 “Welcome to a dying industry” is the advice that Rik van Hemmen, as a young professional starting with Martin & Ottaway, received from a group of grizzled veterans at an industry event in New York City. But van Hemmen is the furthest from a conventional thinker, so he thanked them for their advice, pointed out that they were old, they would be gone soon and whatever was left was his. Though his maritime journey is long, as a young man van Hemmen was not convinced that maritime was his future, despite the fact that he’s a literal “Son of a son of a Sailor”, with both his father and grandfather working a ship’s engineers in The Netherlands. Emigrating from the Netherlands as a teen, van Hemmen found his path studying Aerospace and Ocean Engineering at Virginia Tech, along the way working for: a defense contractor; the American Bureau of Shipping as a surveyor; designing America’s Cup sailboats; eventually joining Martin & Ottaway – which this year celebrated its 150th anniversary – where his father was a partner. Through his engineering career of studying maritime failures, van Hemmen has amassed many insights and stories on the industry that is his home, stories shared regularly in Maritime Reporter & Engineering News, and now here with Maritime Matters: The MarineLink Podcast.

articles.title: Gulf Congestion Rises, Fujairah Takes 28%
articles.summary: Fujairah records the largest concentration of waiting bulk vessels. articles.body: Gulf Congestion Rises, Fujairah Takes 28% in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 Fujairah records the largest concentration of waiting bulk vessels. More than six months into the Middle East shipping crisis, vessel waiting remains elevated across the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. As of 28 October, 265 dry bulk vessels were recorded waiting across 29 selected ports, led by Fujairah with 74 vessels (28%) and Sohar with 50. Together, the two ports account for 47% of the regional waiting fleet. Supramax represents the largest segment, with 107 vessels (40%), followed by Panamax (56) and Handysize (53). Prolonged waiting, particularly among Supramax vessels, can reduce prompt tonnage availability, although the freight impact depends on waiting duration and subsequent vessel employment. Regional waiting is running 75% above last year. The regional waiting series averaged 268 vessels in 1–27 October, against 154 in the same period of 2025 and 139 in 2024. The count dipped to 170 in mid-July, rebuilt through August to a peak of 291 on 15 September, and stood at 254 on 27 October. Inside Fujairah: Supramax Accounts for Half of Waiting Dry Bulk Vessels Supramax dominates Fujairah’s waiting fleet. Of the 74 vessels recorded waiting on 28 October, 37 were Supramaxes, representing 50% of the port’s total compared with 40% across the wider 29-port region. Fujairah alone accounts for nearly 35% of all waiting Supramaxes in the regional sample, while Panamax and Handysize follow with 12 vessels each. Stop calls dominate vessel activity. Of the 74 waiting vessels, 48 (65%) are classified as stop calls, compared with 22 for discharge and just four for loading. This contrasts with the wider regional pattern, where discharge accounts for 109 vessels and stops for 102. Fujairah consequently represents almost half of all regional waiting stop calls, suggesting that its vessel accumulation extends beyond conventional loading and discharge activity. Congestion has intensified since mid-year. Fujairah’s daily waiting count remained largely below 40 vessels during the first half of 2026 before rising through July and August. The fleet subsequently reached approximately 80–95 vessels during September and October, before easing to 74 by 28 October. Despite the recent moderation, waiting levels remain elevated compared with the first half of the year. SPOTLIGHT OF THE WEEK | FUJAIRAH Capesize iron ore routes and Asian Supramax tightened, Panamax Atlantic shortfalls deepened, while Handysize HS7 (North China) and Panamax P6 moved into balance; HS6 remains in surplus. The US Gulf remains oversupplied for Supramax. FREIGHT MARKET OVERVIEW From Week 42 to Week 43. Week 42 was a heavy week for Capesize: the BCI fell 975 points to 3,365, and C5TC(180) dropped to $27,015/day, pulling the BDI down 406 points to 2,511. The previous week, the market recovered part of that loss. The BDI rose 149 points to 2,660 as the BCI regained 361 points and C5TC(180) climbed to $30,292/day. Supramax and Handysize kept their steady climb (BHSI at a 52-week high), while Panamax fell for a second week, with P5TC down from $20,827 to $18,981/day. Smaller sizes lead. The geared segments are the steadiest part of the market: the BHSI is at a 52-week high, and the BSI is 3 points below its own, with HS3_38 (South Atlantic) +$1,550 and Supramax S3 (North China–West Africa) +$2,050 this week. KEY TAKEAWAY • Capesize rates recovered a portion of their Week 42 declines as vessel availability tightened relative to cargo demand on the C3 and C5 iron ore routes. • Asian Supramax markets strengthened amid regional tonnage scarcity. Conversely, Panamax stood out as a clear exception, dropping for a second consecutive week despite expectations of a deficit in forward vessel supply; a growing ballast fleet in the South Atlantic may be adding downside pressure. Geared tonnage remains oversupplied in the US Gulf. • Across 29 Middle Eastern ports, 265 vessels are currently waiting—74 at Fujairah, mostly Supramaxes, and mostly on stop calls. With regional congestion running 75% above last year’s levels, available geared tonnage outside the Strait of Hormuz could face persistent operational constraints as long as these ships remain idle. CAPESIZE Freight. The BCI rose 361 points to 3,726 and C5TC(180) $3,277 to $30,292/day (C5TC(182) $33,795). The Pacific led: C10_182 +$7,163 to $35,868/day and C5 +$1.49 to $13.94/mt. C3 gained $2.92 to $33.64/mt, and C14_182 gained $4,546 to $33,064/day; C8_182 fell $1,850 to $29,550/day. C9_182 remains the top route at $64,200/day. Ships vs cargoes. On C3, there are now fewer ships than cargoes for about the next 30 days, evening out only around day 40 (~330 each), against about 16 days in the previous reading. On C5, ships fall short of cargoes between days 6 and 14. Australasia ballasters fell 21% while FEAST/NOPAC rose 29%, so open tonnage is shifting north rather than disappearing. PANAMAX Freight. The BPI fell 205 points to 2,109 and P5TC fell from $1,846 to $18,981/day, with all routes lower. The Atlantic led the fall: P1A_82 −$2,809 to $17,736/day and P2A_82 −$2,577 to $26,520/day (still the top route); P6_82 −$2,455. P7 and P8 eased to $71.94/mt and $53.69/mt. Ships vs cargoes. Forward vessel supply continues to lag behind expected demand across the P1/P2/P7 (~63 vessels against ~102 by day 20), P3, and P5 routes, whereas P6 has approached market balance. Despite these ongoing deficit conditions, freight rates trended lower. Although an influx of ballasters into the South Atlantic (+25%) and Indian Ocean/South Africa region (+7%). The divergence between forward supply–demand balances and declining freight rates suggests that the projected shortages have yet to translate into sustained support for earnings. SUPRAMAX Freight. The BSI edged up 22 points to 1,887, just below its 52-week high of 1,890, and S11TC $276 to $23,849/day. Asia led: S3 +$2,050 to $24,167/day, S8 +$514 to $27,900/day and S10 +$456. The US Gulf eased: S1C −$1,475 to $30,169/day and S4A −$1,066 to $30,853/day (still the top route). Ships vs cargoes. The US Gulf routes (S4A/S1C, S4B) still have more ships than cargoes, and North Atlantic ballasters jumped 38% to 113. In Asia (S8/S10), ships fall short of cargoes throughout (~111 vs ~128 by day 10), and West Africa (S5) is short for the first ~16 days. HANDYSIZE Freight. The BHSI rose 9 points to 1,020, a 52-week high, and HS7TC rose from $161 to $18,361/day. HS3_38 (South Atlantic) gained $1,550 to $30,022/day and remains the top route; HS4_38 (US Gulf) fell $772 to $19,657/day. Asia firmed modestly (HS5 +$200, HS6 and HS7 +$163). Ships vs cargoes. HS1/HS2, HS5 and HS6 all have more ships than cargoes. HS7, where ships were short of cargoes in the previous reading, is now balanced (~158 vs ~157 by day 10). Global ballasters rose 15% to 686, with gains in every region, which caps further upside. articles.body: Ship Recycling Market: Steady as She Goes in Hellenic Shipping News 30/10/2026 T he ship recycling market has remained broadly stable over the past few days. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships said that “the Indian ship recycling market continues to remain stable, supported by healthy local steel consumption and steady demand for recycled steel. The availability of vessels for recycling remains extremely limited, with very few suitable candidates currently entering the market. Market participants are closely monitoring reports of a recent U.S. government circular concerning the potential removal of OFAC sanctions on certain vessels, which could create additional recycling opportunities. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, with favourable local steel market conditions supporting buying interest despite the shortage of available tonnage”. Source: Best Oasis The company’s report added that “the Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to remain soft, although buying interest remains strong, with buyers actively seeking suitable vessels for recycling. The availability of recycling tonnage remains extremely limited, with very few vessels currently being offered for sale. Despite subdued market conditions, buyers remain keen to secure available tonnage, with the continued shortage of vessels restricting overall transaction activity. Overall, market sentiment remains cautious, while strong buying interest and limited vessel availability continue to characterise the market. The Pakistani ship recycling market has witnessed mixed movements compared to last week, although buyers continue to maintain strong purchasing capacity and keen interest in acquiring vessels. The reported closure of the Iran–Pakistan border has brought steel and rebar imports from Iran to a complete halt, following a significant reduction in supplies over recent weeks. This disruption in steel imports has provided a positive boost to the local ship recycling industry, as reduced availability of imported steel supports demand for locally recycled steel. Overall, buying interest remains strong, with restricted steel imports providing additional support to the local recycling market despite some fluctuations in market conditions. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market remains stable, with limited trading activity and no significant changes reported during the week. The Turkish lira continues to remain weak, although currency fluctuations have not resulted in any further impact on recycling prices for the time being. Vessel availability remains influenced by EU regulations and the supply of suitable recycling candidates trading within or positioned near the region. Overall, Turkish recycling yards remain relatively busy and selective in their purchasing approach, with buying interest primarily focused on well-positioned and commercially attractive vessels that meet their specific requirements”, Best Oasis concluded. Meanwhile, in a separate weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “last week, recycling markets held broadly steady, except Pakistan and Bangladesh, which retain their strong appetite despite subdued market conditions. Alang remained stable, maintaining last week’s positive sentiment amid the festive period. Local steel plate prices firmed, even as holiday closures slowed demand. Exchangerate movements have been comparatively contained. Buying interest is selective and recycling activity remains limited, with general cargo and reefer arrivals at the waterfront alongside previously secured tankers and large specialist units. On the policy front, authorized ship recycling facilities by the Gujarat Maritime Board reached 47, a significant step towards yard compliance. Chattogram remains soft, although buying interest is still strong. Local steel market is broadly stable, as festival holidays slowed down momentum. Steel mills are cautious and are holding minimal stock, though this could change as construction picks up seasonally. Source: Intermodal Shipbroker Local currency weakened against USD and candidate pool remains limited. On the macro side, slowing economy has curbed loan demand and left banks with surplus liquidity, creating better financing opportunities for recyclers. Pakistan showed mixed signals, with buying interest remaining strong, despite trade restrictions. Local steel prices declined, affected by weak demand. Local currency was unchanged against the dollar. Tonnage arrivals have been steady, but the wider market remains supply-constrained, keeping purchasing appetite balanced. Attention is focused on the closure of borders with Iran, as this disruption halted Iranian steel and rebar imports and will offer breakers a measure of support. Aliaga remained unchanged. Local steel prices corrected modestly with mills being cautious and facing liquidity constraints. Lira continues to weaken against USD and recycling flows are slow. The central bank cut its policy rate from 37% to 36%, offering modest financing relief, although present market conditions continue to limit buying capacity”, Intermodal concluded. articles.title: Dry Bulk Shipping: Escalating attacks on ships heighten uncertainty
articles.summary: “Geopolitical disruptions continue to cloud the dry bulk market outlook. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz remains the largest source of uncertainty, while attacks on ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea have added another layer of risk,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO....
articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Escalating attacks on ships heighten uncertainty in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 30/10/2026 “G eopolitical disruptions continue to cloud the dry bulk market outlook. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz remains the largest source of uncertainty, while attacks on ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea have added another layer of risk,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. Typically, around 4% of dry bulk demand sails via the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have softened the impact of the disruption but have been unable to replace pre-war volumes. The disruption has also tightened energy and fertiliser supplies, weighing on global economic growth and raising concerns over food security. Given the uncertainty, BIMCO presents two forecast scenarios. The “SoH closed” scenario assumes that the strait remains effectively closed throughout 2027 and 2028, while the “SoH open” scenario assumes that ships can freely transit the strait from 2027 onwards. “We expect the dry bulk supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, although from a high baseline. Cargo volume growth is expected to be limited, while ship deliveries accelerate, particularly in the capesize segment,” says Gouveia. In 2027, ship demand is forecast to grow 0.5-2.5% if the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed, compared with supply growth of 3-4%. If the strait reopens, both demand and supply growth are expected to be 1 percentage point higher. In this scenario, demand would grow faster for commodities other than coal supported by improved economic conditions and stronger import demand from countries in the Persian Gulf. However, the fleet currently trapped in the Gulf would begin operating as normal and sailing speeds could remain slightly higher than in our other scenario, increasing supply. In 2028, ship demand is forecast to grow 0.5-2.5% in both scenarios, while supply is expected to grow 3-4%. Cargo volume growth is expected to remain limited as coal shipments decline, while the return of bulkers to the Panama Canal could weigh on average sailing distance growth. On the supply side, rising ship deliveries are expected to support strong fleet growth, even as ship recycling increases. Lastly, average sailing speeds are expected to decrease slightly as market conditions soften. “Disruptions to Black Sea shipping pose an additional downside risk to the market outlook. The forecast assumes that Russian and Ukrainian grain volumes unable to be shipped in 2026 are instead exported in 2027. If they remain unavailable, dry bulk cargo growth could be up to 0.5 percentage points weaker in 2027 and grain shipment growth up to 4 percentage points weaker,” says Gouveia. articles.title: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market
articles.summary: China’s property slump has turned Asia’s cement trade inside out. The cargo has not grown much, but it now travels much further, and Supramaxes are doing most of the extra work. From buyer to seller Not long ago, China was where Vietnam sent its clinker. In 2020 some 36 Mt went there, mostly on short ...
articles.body: Shifts in cement trade help support the Supramax market in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 China’s property slump has turned Asia’s cement trade inside out. The cargo has not grown much, but it now travels much further, and Supramaxes are doing most of the extra work. From buyer to seller Not long ago, China was where Vietnam sent its clinker. In 2020 some 36 Mt went there, mostly on short hops from northern Vietnam to southern China, ideal work for Handysizes and Supramaxes shuttling back and forth. Then the property market broke. Building stalled, demand for cement fell away, and Chinese kilns were left running at around half capacity. By 2025 China’s imports had all but vanished. What happened next is the real story. With too much clinker and too few buyers at home, Chinese producers went looking abroad. Exports climbed from under a million tonnes in 2022 to a forecast 24.6 Mt this year, and we expect them to hold above 21 Mt through 2028. About two-thirds of this year’s flow is clinker, the bulk intermediate that grinding mills turn into cement, and it is heading further afield: to Bangladesh, the Philippines and, increasingly, West Africa. That is Supramax business. Vietnam goes further afield Vietnam lost its biggest customer almost overnight, so it did what any exporter would: it found new ones, further away. Its exports are a mix of roughly 60% cement and 40% clinker, and this year the average cargo looks set to travel about three times as far as it did in 2019. Handysizes still handle the regional runs to the Philippines and Bangladesh, but the long-haul tail goes on Supramaxes and Ultramaxes. Neighbours have not made it easy, with Taiwan and the Philippines both putting up barriers to Vietnamese cement. From 2027 we see some of that long-haul business fading as Chinese clinker competes for the same buyers. The US: longer, not bigger The US shows the pattern most clearly. It is not importing much more cement than a few years ago; it is importing it from much further away. Turkey and Vietnam have taken share from closer suppliers, and the average cargo now sails about 6,800 nm, up from about 5,250 nm in 2019. These are Supramax-sized parcels on some of the longest routes in the trade, and the new 50% tariff on Canadian cement may stretch them further. We see volumes steady at around 22 to 24 Mt a year to 2028, with the voyages staying long. Distance does the work Put the main exporters together and the picture is simple. They are shipping about a quarter more cement than in 2019, but the tonne-miles have doubled. The voyage times make the point. The old Vietnam to China run took about 13 days round trip, port time included. Vietnam to the US Gulf takes a Supramax about 88 days, and China to West Africa about 75. So every million tonnes that moves from the short route to a long one ties up around four more ships for a year, and across the trade the extra distance since 2019 is worth the full-time work of around 110 Supramaxes in 2026. Because the long hauls go on the bigger ships, Supramax tonne-miles in cement from China and Vietnam look set to rise by more than 80% this year, against about a third for Handysizes. Many of these ships ballast home, though some voyages can be linked to a backhaul such as petcoke for which cement plants are a major consumer. Europe’s carbon border A second force is at work, and this one starts in Brussels. High energy costs made Europe an importer of clinker, the energy-hungry stage of cement making. EU imports grew roughly sixfold between 2016 and 2025, mostly on short runs from Turkey and North Africa. Since January the EU’s carbon border charge has put a price on the carbon in that clinker, and European producers want it tightened. Importers stocked up ahead of the start date, and Turkish clinker has already begun turning towards West Africa and the Americas. For Supramaxes, that is another shift from short haul to long. A round voyage from Turkey to Ghana takes about 44 days, against 18 to Italy. Building the trade away None of this lasts forever, and China may be what ends it. Chinese engineering groups, led by Sinoma, are building cement plants across Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean, and Sinoma’s overseas orders doubled in the second quarter of this year. Every new kiln in West Africa means less imported clinker. In effect, China is exporting first the cargo and then the factory that replaces it while building Chinese economic influence through its inward investment. Support for the Supramax market So what does it add up to? Construction cargoes, led by cement and clinker, make up around 8% of Supramax demand. This year they are the largest single source of new work in the segment, ahead of South American grain and iron ore, and they roughly cancel out the loss from coal in Southeast Asia. Cement on its own does not set the market, but it helps at the margin. When a fleet is close to fully employed, small changes in demand can have an outsized effect on rates, so the extra miles look supportive for Supramax earnings through 2026. The support fades in 2027 as hauls shorten, then levels out in 2028. Handysizes feel it less, because more of their cement work stays close to home. That is the nature of cement: a local business at heart, with seaborne trade filling the gaps while capacity catches up. Right now the gaps are large, and a long way from the surplus. Our view China is the catalyst. Its building slump has turned a short-haul regional trade into a long-haul one. In our view cement tonne-days peak in 2026, ease a little in 2027 and stay around twice their 2019 level through 2028. Supramaxes gain most: cement is a useful prop for their earnings this year, fading in 2027. ▪ Upside: Chinese capacity cuts come slower than planned, and tariffs or Europe’s carbon border push more cargo onto long routes. ▪ Downside: Beijing removes its surplus faster, more countries shut out imports, or new plants in Africa and the Middle East start up sooner. Most uncertain call: how long China keeps exporting at this pace. Even a modest recovery at home would pull tonnes back quickly. Data note Tradeviews research. articles.title: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes
articles.summary: On the same trade, the choice of carrier can change a voyage’s Well-to-Wake (WtW) emissions intensity by as much as 35%, according to Decoding Maritime Emissions, Q3 2026: Stable Intensity, Diverging Voyage Performance, VesselBot’s latest quarterly report. Across the carriers compared on four major fronthaul trades,...
articles.body: Same Trade Lane, Different Footprint: Carrier Emissions Intensity Differs by Up to 35% on Major Container Routes in Hellenic Shipping News 30/10/2026 O n the same trade, the choice of carrier can change a voyage’s Well-to-Wake (WtW) emissions intensity by as much as 35%, according to Decoding Maritime Emissions, Q3 2026: Stable Intensity, Diverging Voyage Performance, VesselBot’s latest quarterly report. Across the carriers compared on four major fronthaul trades, the gap between the most and least efficient ranged from 20% to 35%, while fleet-wide average intensity remained broadly stable at 235.1 g CO₂e/TEU-km (+0.5% year over year). The report also shows why absolute emissions are a poor measure of efficiency. On the China/East Asia–Northern Europe trade, the carrier with the lowest emissions intensity, out of the three carriers examined, also recorded the highest average emissions per voyage, highlighting the importance of cargo volumes and vessel utilization when assessing environmental performance. Based on an analysis of 83,817 voyages performed by 6,730 container-carrying vessels, the report examines how actual vessel operations, including sailing patterns, port stays, cargo utilization and vessel deployment, influence maritime emissions performance. The findings highlight the importance of looking beyond aggregate figures to understand the operational conditions shaping transportation efficiency. Key findings from the report • Stable intensity masks diverging performance. Total emissions fell 1.9% year over year to 55.5 mn tonnes CO₂e while transport work rose 1.2% to 712 bn TEU-km. Average WtW intensity stayed broadly stable at 235.1 g CO₂e/TEU-km (+0.5%). Tracked voyages fell 2.8%, and average voyage duration rose to 5.3 days, the highest of the first three quarters of 2026. • Five of six vessel-size categories improved their intensity, while Feeders continued to move in the opposite direction. Year-over-year improvements ranged from 3.4% for Panamax to 12.9% for VLCS, but Feeder intensity rose 1.3% to 285.9 g CO₂e/TEU-km. With Feeders accounting for 65% of all voyages, the findings illustrate why a broadly stable fleet-wide average can conceal different performance trends across vessel categories. • The gradual return to the Suez Canal has yet to materially shorten Asia–Europe voyages. The Suez Canal Authority reports 166 medium and large containerships transiting between July and September 2026, up from 16 a year earlier. Yet average durations on China/East Asia–Northern Europe (33.2 days) and China/East Asia–Mediterranean (29.7 days) remained close to Q3 2025 and Q2 2026 levels, as most voyages still used the Cape of Good Hope route. • Port time increased across every vessel size, with some trade lanes experiencing substantially larger rises. Average port time per voyage rose 6.2% to 27.3% year over year across vessel categories, with VLCS recording the largest increase, to 2.9 days. On the Northern Europe–North America East Coast trade, port time jumped 52.1% to 2.1 days. Longer port stays can reduce emissions efficiency, because vessels keep consuming fuel without generating additional transport work. • Higher emissions per voyage did not necessarily mean lower efficiency. On direct China/East Asia–Northern Europe voyages, Evergreen recorded the highest average emissions of the three carriers examined (14,273 tonnes CO₂e), yet achieved the lowest intensity, at 47.4 g CO₂e/TEU-km, about 17% below the trade average of 57.3. Its voyages carried 20,400 TEU on average at 96% utilization. Assessing efficiency requires looking at cargo volume and operating conditions, not absolute emissions alone. • Utilization and vessel size drive efficiency. Voyages below 50 g CO₂e/TEU-km averaged 80% utilization, against 32% for those at or above 800 g. Of the 2,226 highest-intensity voyages, 2,012 (90%) were operated by Feeder and Panamax vessels. At the same time, NeoPanamax and VLCS made up just 7% of voyages but generated 43% of transport work. Beyond emissions measurement: understanding what drives performance VesselBot’s analysis combines AIS-based vessel tracking with vessel-specific digital twin models to estimate fuel consumption and Well-to-Wake emissions at voyage level. This approach enables the company to examine performance across vessels, carriers, routes and operational conditions, rather than relying exclusively on published emission factors or aggregate carrier data. The findings also illustrate the distinction between benchmarking performance and estimating the emissions of a particular shipment. While industry, trade and carrier averages help identify trends, shipment-specific execution data and fuel-consumption modeling provide a more granular basis for understanding transportation performance and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency. “An average emissions figure may tell us whether the overall market is improving or deteriorating, but it cannot explain what is happening on individual voyages,” said Constantine Komodromos, Founder and CEO of VesselBot. “In Q3, we observed relatively stable fleet-wide intensity alongside longer port stays and meaningful differences in carrier efficiency. By examining vessel deployment, actual sailing patterns, cargo utilization and time spent at sea and in port, we can identify what drives those outcomes. For shippers, that distinction matters because emissions data should do more than support reporting. It should provide the evidence needed to evaluate carriers, understand operational inefficiencies and make better transportation decisions.” The full report, Decoding Maritime Emissions, Q3 2026: Stable Intensity, Diverging Voyage Performance, is available here . The findings highlight the importance of looking beyond aggregate figures to understand the operational conditions shaping transportation efficiency.

articles.title: Crude Freight: Past the Peak, But the Floor Should Hold
articles.summary: VLCC rates from the US Gulf and West Africa have fallen from historical peaks by 27% and 32% respectively over the past two weeks, with smaller tankers following. Is this a short-term correction, or the start of a deeper decline? And if rates fall further, would they reach pre-war levels? To answer that, we need ...
articles.body: Crude Freight: Past the Peak, But the Floor Should Hold in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 VLCC rates from the US Gulf and West Africa have fallen from historical peaks by 27% and 32% respectively over the past two weeks, with smaller tankers following. Is this a short-term correction, or the start of a deeper decline? And if rates fall further, would they reach pre-war levels? To answer that, we need to look at the five main drivers of this year’s rally: 1. Middle East Gulf (MEG) ship-to-ship (STS) shuttle relay delays, which tie up tonnage and tighten the Atlantic Basin 2. War risk premia 3. The shift of trade flows from sanctioned to mainstream markets 4. Market consolidation 5. Higher bunker costs Bunker costs have doubled this year relatively in tandem with oil prices. That has naturally raised the floor for tanker rates, but it does not fully explain a tenfold rise in freight. This article therefore focuses on the first four factors. Atlantic Basin availability is tight, but current freight levels still make flows to Asia unattractive The recent drop in Atlantic Basin rates is triggered from charterers stepping back from the market. Atlantic crude discounts are at record levels, but high freight still makes trades to Asia uneconomic. In October, the freight premium for moving Atlantic-origin crude to Asia on VLCCs, compared with cargoes from the East of Hormuz, is at least five times what it was in 2025. Atlantic VLCCs have also lost pricing power against Atlantic Suezmaxes. Moving an Atlantic cargo east on a VLCC rather than a Suezmax now costs about $8/bl more on average, against around $1.50/bl a year ago. These weaker netbacks for Asian refiners have softened the VLCC enquiries in the Atlantic. Additionally, with VLCC fixing activity muted over the past 10 days, the tonnage list is lengthening, with the number of VLCC ballasters heading to the Atlantic Basin up by 30% over the same period. That is however still 20% below 2025 levels. VLCC availability could also increase further. As VLCC demand shifts towards the Middle East and away from the Atlantic, future tonne-miles to Asia are likely to shorten. Over the next month, vessels now carrying barrels to Asia will discharge and become available again. Crude arrivals into Asia on VLCCs and Suezmaxes are projected at 23.3 mbd this week and over the next two weeks, about 1.5 mbd above the 2025 average. Laden mainstream VLCCs and Suezmaxes currently located in East Asia are up 15% since the start of September. The prospective stronger-than-average discharges have a two-fold effect. They release more tonnage into the market, and they ease short-term destocking concerns in Asia. Both bearish factors for freight in the near future. Potential OFAC sanctions relief could bring limited additional tonnage to mainstream trades As discussed in previous articles, the shift of crude flows away from sanctioned origins, mainly Iran, towards the international market has been a key driver of freight. This holds only while vessels engaged in sanctioned trades remain barred from mainstream employment. That barrier may soon ease. The US is considering a waiver that would allow tankers sanctioned for links to Russia, Iran or Venezuela to carry non-sanctioned oil, or to be sold to mainstream owners. In theory, this could release meaningful tonnage. In practice, the impact is likely to be limited. All but five OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs are either already active or directly tied to Iran, which makes it uncertain whether these tankers would apply for a waiver. Among actively trading VLCCs, only two are aged 15–20 years and have no Iranian links. A 20-year age limit has long been a standard threshold in the vetting and chartering policies of oil majors and national producers. Vessels that have spent years without access to reputable repair yards or classification society oversight are likely to face even stricter scrutiny, depending on their intended employment. As a result, these tankers are more likely to be deployed in shuttle trades around Hormuz or on MEG–Asia routes, freeing up mainstream tonnage to reposition towards the Atlantic Basin. The same is true for smaller tankers. Only 2 Suezmaxes and 2 Aframaxes, that traditionally serve European demand on Atlantic routes, are not sanctioned by the EU or UK and also have no Iranian ties and are not actively employed. Based on the illustration below, the most likely candidates for a return to mainstream trade are relatively young vessels without Iranian links: 7 VLCCs, 14 Suezmaxes and 58 Aframax/LR2s. In an edge case where Iran-linked young tankers also apply for and receive waivers, this rises to 48 VLCCs, 27 Suezmaxes and 65 Aframaxes. If tankers do apply for waivers, or mainstream owners take the risk of buying them, this could partly ease rates. The effect would not be immediate, though. The age of these vessels means maintenance, inspections and insurance could delay their return, and commercial requirements would make any re-entry gradual. Tonnage increases but vessel requirements and inefficiencies continue strong Does this signal a sharp downwards correction in freight? Unlikely. Attacks on shipping around the Middle East have not eased. In October they reached a record of 29 vessel incidents around Hormuz, according to IMO. We currently count 18 non-Iranian VLCCs likely out of operation since the start of the conflict, which is equal to around 2-3% of the mainstream VLCC fleet, a non-insignificant portion. Furthermore, despite these attacks, flows continue through both single voyages and STS chains. More than half of West of Hormuz seaborne crude exports, about 6mbd, is moving via STS, occupying around 30 VLCCs on average as shuttle tankers (vessels with at least two laden outbound transits in the past three months). In October, India West Coast gained share as an STS zone. This shows the market adapting to labour and equipment shortages (and fearful of attacks), by expanding operations to new locations. Both ways of moving oil out of the Hormuz strait remain inefficient. Both in September and in October, a single voyage takes around 10 days from entering the Gulf to exiting it. A shuttle tanker needs 12–13 days from entering the Strait to completing an STS in the Gulf of Oman. Middle East crude exports, excluding Iran, have now surpassed their historical averages of around 16mbd. With Yanbu exports back, able to relieve export pressure for Saudi Arabia from the Red Sea, seaborne exports from West of Hormuz via the strait could stabilise at current levels of 10-11mbd. The constraint is not a shortage of vessels in the region relative to exports, but how fast these vessels can load. As long as these delays persist and STS operations remain significant relative to direct voyages, tonnage will stay tied up in the region and continue to support rates. Beyond the region, tanker ownership is also becoming more concentrated. On VLCCs, the top 10 operators alongside the major independent trading houses as well as the Middle Eastern and Asian state-owned companies together control 67% of the mainstream fleet (4% increase y-o-y, 10% since 2021). The state-owned companies and traders are increasingly managing their own freight risk, keeping part of the fleet off the open market. More broadly, consolidation gives a smaller group of players more pricing power. By limiting the effectively available fleet, they can command higher rates, which provides a floor during downturns. Conclusion Tanker freight looks to have peaked, at least in the short-term. More available crude tanker tonnage is coming to market as cargoes discharge in Asia, ballast voyages shorten and sanctioned vessels potentially return. A return to pre-war levels is also still unlikely. Loading delays in the Middle East continue to tie up vessels. Persistent delays could drive more vessels to the Atlantic, putting further pressure initially on rates but making Atlantic barrels once more attractive relative to the Middle East, thus putting a floor subsequently, especially if war risk premia around Hormuz remain at record highs. A more consolidated market also gives operators greater leverage, which adds to the pricing floor, at a time where crude inventories in Asian importing countries could reduce draw rates because of historically high levels of arrivals but these will not end up in significant build-ups. Objecting to the inclusion of facilities that comply with the stringent EU safety and environmental standards would undermine the credibility of the EU’s own legislation”, said Sotiris Raptis, Secretary General of European Shipowners | ECSA. articles.summary: India has the potential to become a competitive regional hub for alternative marine fuels, according to the Study on Potential Demand and Pricing of Alternative Marine Fuels in India. Initiated by India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW),...
articles.body: IMO: Study Identifies A Phased Pathway For India To Develop A Competitive Regional Alternative Marine Fuel Hub in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 India has the potential to become a competitive regional hub for alternative marine fuels, according to the Study on Potential Demand and Pricing of Alternative Marine Fuels in India. Initiated by India’s Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW), and supported through IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 Programme, the study examines future demand for alternative marine fuels, fuel pricing and the practical steps needed to strengthen India’s competitiveness in the emerging alternative marine fuel market. Competitiveness will drive future bunkering decisions One of the study’s key findings is that competitiveness, rather than geography alone, will determine where ships choose to bunker in the future. Factors such as delivered fuel costs, operational efficiency, reliability and port charges are likely to be decisive. The analysis indicates that India could compete regionally across all major alternative fuel pathways, with demand of biofuels and methanol expected to support earlier uptake, followed by ammonia as supply chains, infrastructure and safety frameworks mature. Realizing this potential will depend on the country’s ability to provide an attractive overall bunkering proposition, supported by efficient port operations, clear regulatory procedures, reliable fuel supplies and predictable costs. Shri Shyam Jagannathan, Director General of Maritime Administration, Government of India, said: “The transition to alternative marine fuels presents a significant opportunity for India. Beyond supporting the decarbonization of shipping, it can strengthen our energy security, reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, create new industrial opportunities and reinforce India’s position as a leading maritime nation.” Leveraging existing traffic to build demand The study also concludes that India’s strongest opportunity lies in serving ships already calling at its ports, rather than primarily seeking to attract transiting traffic. To support market development, the study recommends concentrating initial efforts at a limited number of strategic ports, including Mundra, JNPT, Chennai and Tuticorin, where strong cargo volumes and established shipping activity create favorable conditions for commercially viable bunkering operations. It proposes a three-phase pathway: establishing safe and competitive bunkering at selected ports in 2026-2030; scaling proven operations and preparing for ammonia bunkering in 2030-2035; and positioning India for multi-fuel bunkering and green shipping corridors in 2035-2047. Methanol is identified as the most suitable starting fuel, with a potential first pilot at Mundra supplied from Deendayal (Kandla). Supporting the development of India’s National Green Shipping Policy Building on the GreenVoyage2050 Policy and Investment Dialogue on Alternative Marine Fuels and Bunkering Competitiveness held earlier in the year, the findings provide timely evidence and practical recommendations to support the ongoing development of India’s National Green Shipping Policy, which aims to accelerate the decarbonization of the country’s maritime sector while enhancing its competitiveness and promoting sustainable economic growth. articles.title: DP World launches logistics hub in Italy
articles.summary: DP World has launched its first Fast Moving Consumer Goods contract logistics operation in Italy, opening a 22,000 square metre temperature-controlled, multi-customer facility at Castel San Pietro Terme near Bologna. The hub is designed to serve customers across the food and beverage industry, e-commerce and consumer...
articles.body: DP World has launched its first Fast Moving Consumer Goods contract logistics operation in Italy, opening a 22,000 square metre temperature-controlled, multi-customer facility at Castel San Pietro Terme near Bologna. The hub is designed to serve customers across the food and beverage industry, e-commerce and consumer goods sectors, combining warehousing, transport, e-commerce fulfilment and value-added logistics services to provide integrated end-to-end supply chain solutions for customers in Italy and across Europe. The operation was established through a strategic partnership with Alce Nero, an Italian organic food company that serves as the site’s anchor customer. Under the arrangement, DP World manages key elements of Alce Nero’s logistics operations including warehousing, e-commerce fulfilment and transportation. The facility features temperature-controlled storage at 18 to 20 degrees Celsius, organic product handling capabilities and integrated logistics technology, with approximately 30,000 pallet positions and capacity to support additional customers beyond the anchor tenant. Its location near Bologna provides access to Italy’s domestic market and major European transport corridors. Rainer Schmid, CCO of DP World Europe, described the Italian launch as an important milestone and characterised the Alce Nero partnership as exemplifying the company’s growth approach of starting with a specific customer need, building the right solution around it and creating capabilities that can subsequently serve other businesses in the market. Renzo Patelli, General Manager of Alce Nero, described finding the right logistics partner as an important process given the complexity of the company’s business model spanning multiple supply chains, channels and customer requirements, and expressed confidence that the partnership will make logistics operations more efficient, flexible and responsive while allowing Alce Nero to focus on its core organic food business.

articles.body: The Management Committee of the Southern Tyrrhenian and Ionian Sea Port System Authority has adopted the 2027 Budget forecast and the 2027-2029 Three-Year Public Works Programme, outlining a significant investment programme across the system’s five Calabrian ports. The 2027 budget shows revenues of approximately EUR 24 million and estimated expenditures of approximately EUR 88 million, with capital expenditures of EUR 70 million in addition to EUR 70 million already included in the current financial year, bringing the combined total to EUR 140 million. The operating deficit of approximately EUR 64 million is fully covered by an estimated operating surplus exceeding EUR 137 million. The most significant single investment in the Three-Year Programme is the completion of the cold ironing system at the Port of Gioia Tauro through the implementation of an already contracted Framework Agreement, representing a further EUR 30 million investment. Also at Gioia Tauro, a tender is expected to be launched for the development of the former Isotta Fraschini area, earmarked for the construction of a new rail-ship-road interchange at a cost of EUR 10 million, strengthening integration between maritime and rail transport and connecting the port to national and European logistics corridors. Environmental redevelopment of the port’s internal areas and beach, including the former greenhouse area south of the port, is planned to begin in 2027 at a total investment of EUR 5 million. Across the ports of Crotone, Corigliano Calabro and Vibo Valentia, energy efficiency projects totalling EUR 2.5 million will improve infrastructure efficiency, install renewable energy generation capacity and create the conditions for the development of Renewable Energy Communities, implementing the guidelines of the Port System Energy and Environmental Planning Document. President Paolo Piacenza described the programme as outlining a concrete development perspective for the entire port system, with Gioia Tauro serving as the main logistics and intermodal engine while Crotone, Corigliano Calabro, Vibo Valentia Marina and Taureana di Palmi perform complementary and strategic functions. He characterised the planned investments as a clear strategic choice to improve infrastructure quality, strengthen intermodality, support the energy transition and attract new traffic and economic activity to Calabria.

articles.title: Gulf Oil Producers Build Tanker Fleet as Security Risks Mount Around Hormuz
articles.summary: Gulf oil producers are assembling a fleet of nearly 230 tankers to maintain crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz despite heightened security risks and reluctance among independent shipowners to operate in the region, according to a weekly…
articles.body: Gulf Oil Producers Build Tanker Fleet as Security Risks Mount Around Hormuz Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Three tankers carrying russian diesel to the U.S. © Windward Gulf oil producers are assembling a fleet of nearly 230 tankers to maintain crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz despite heightened security risks and reluctance among independent shipowners to operate in the region, according to a weekly intelligence report from Windward Maritime dated October 29. The report identifies five maritime developments, including changes to Gulf oil transportation, an oil spill threatening infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates, suspicious movements near subsea communications cables, continued Russian oil trading under sanctions pressure and shipping activity through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Gulf states expand their tanker capacity Windward describes the emergence of what it calls the “Arab Dark Fleet,” comprising tankers owned, managed, chartered or controlled by Gulf national oil companies and their trading and shipping affiliates. The fleet allows regional producers to move oil despite elevated freight costs and reduced availability of vessels willing to load at terminals in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the UAE. About 80% of the fleet consists of very large crude carriers (VLCCs). Many operate with their automatic identification systems (AIS) switched off, which Windward says reflects safety and security concerns. The vessels transport crude from terminals west of Hormuz to ship-to-ship transfer hubs off the UAE and Oman, where cargoes are transferred to other tankers for onward delivery. Preliminary Vortexa figures cited by Windward indicate that crude exports, excluding Iranian shipments, from terminals west of Hormuz reached a pace of approximately 11 million barrels per day in October. That compares with 1.56 million barrels per day in May and prewar volumes of 14.5 million barrels per day. The fleet expansion has tied up an estimated 15% to 20% of the global VLCC fleet at any given time, illustrating the scale of the logistical response. Oil spill threatens UAE coastline and desalination infrastructure An oil leak from a tanker anchored approximately 25 kilometers north of Umm Al Quwain reached UAE beaches on October 22, following a forecast issued by Windward two days earlier. Authorities confirmed oil along the coast and closed beaches in Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah on October 23. Ras Al Khaimah closed all its beaches the following day after satellite imagery showed oil along the Al Hamra shoreline. Windward tracked the slick northeast along the coast toward the NAQA’A desalination plant, the largest such facility in the northern emirates. The oil came close enough to the plant’s seawater intake to pose a potential operational threat. As of the report, no desalination plant had reported a shutdown. A service vessel was observed alongside the tanker, although its precise role in containing the leak or offloading cargo remained unclear. Iranian vessels raise concerns over subsea cables Between October 14 and 28, three U.S.-sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing-support vessel made unusual movements near undersea communications cable routes in the Gulf of Oman and off Iran’s Makran coast, according to Windward. The vessels slowed, circled, reversed course or switched off AIS near several cable corridors. One tanker went dark for 86 hours near the 2Africa and Bay of Bengal Gateway routes before reappearing about nine nautical miles from its last reported position. Another turned back toward Oman after slowing near the 2Africa corridor. The activity coincided with statements by Iranian security and military officials threatening regional undersea cables if hostilities resumed. Windward assesses that the vessel movements could indicate cable mapping or preparations for interference, but AIS data alone cannot establish whether the ships conducted surveillance or deployed equipment. Russian oil movements continue despite sanctions Windward also identified a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker discharging approximately 700,000 barrels of Russian ESPO crude at a terminal in Dongying, China, on October 27. The tanker had switched off its AIS signal between October 24 and 28, obscuring its port call. The vessel is sanctioned by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union. Separately, three tankers carrying Russian diesel were reported heading toward the United States under a temporary U.S. sanctions waiver issued on October 9. Windward noted potential compliance challenges involving two of the vessels, which are themselves subject to sanctions. Bab el-Mandeb traffic remains steady Despite continued Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and fighting in Yemen, vessel traffic through Bab el-Mandeb remained broadly stable. Windward recorded an average of 39 daily transits over the three-day period ending October 26, compared with approximately 35 per day since August. Saudi-affiliated vessels were notably scarce, accounting for just 13 of roughly 2,500 crossings tracked between July 20 and October 22. Windward expects these operators to continue avoiding the strait, while other shipowners maintain current transit patterns. Together, the developments highlight the operational adjustments, infrastructure vulnerabilities and sanctions-related complications confronting commercial shipping across the Middle East and beyond.

John Garamendi speaks outside the U.S. Capitol during a press conference with lawmakers, labor leaders and maritime industry representatives urging passage of the SHIPS for America Act, legislation aimed at revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding and the maritime industrial base. A bipartisan group of 119 lawmakers is urging congressional leaders to preserve and expand provisions of the SHIPS for America Act in the final fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), warning that rebuilding the U.S. maritime industry is essential to national and economic security. In an October 29 letter to House and Senate leadership, the lawmakers called for retaining shipbuilding provisions already approved by the House while considering additional measures from the broader legislation that were left out. The letter was led by Representatives Trent Kelly (R-MS) and John Garamendi (D-CA), along with Senators Todd Young (R-IN) and Mark Kelly (D-AZ), the bipartisan sponsors of the SHIPS for America Act. “As negotiations proceed on the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027, we write to share our strong support for the inclusion of the bipartisan, bicameral Shipbuilding and Harbor Infrastructure for Prosperity and Security Act of 2025,” the lawmakers wrote. The push comes as Congress works to finalize the annual defense policy bill, which has emerged as a potential vehicle for advancing long-sought reforms to the U.S. commercial maritime industry. What’s in the SHIPS for America Act? Key Provisions to Restore U.S. Maritime Power The House-passed NDAA, H.R. 8800, includes elements of the SHIPS for America Act under Title XXXVI. According to the letter, those provisions were agreed to unanimously in the House. But the lawmakers argue that the measures represent only a starting point. “The inclusion of these provisions is a necessary start for revitalizing the U.S. maritime industry,” they wrote, adding that Congress should give further consideration to provisions omitted from the House-passed bill. The SHIPS for America Act is a sweeping proposal aimed at reversing decades of decline in American commercial shipbuilding and shipping. It seeks to establish long-term federal maritime policy and oversight, improve the competitiveness of U.S.-flagged vessels in international commerce, rebuild domestic shipyards, and expand recruitment, training, and retention of American mariners and shipyard workers. The lawmakers pointed to the enormous gap between U.S. shipbuilding capacity and that of its Asian competitors. China, South Korea, and Japan collectively account for more than 90% of global shipbuilding by tonnage, while the United States builds less than 1%, according to figures cited in the letter. The lawmakers also noted that fewer than 100 U.S.-flagged vessels participate in international commerce, compared with an estimated Chinese fleet of more than 5,500 ships. That imbalance, they argued, poses risks that extend well beyond commercial competition. “Especially should the United States enter a prolonged conflict, a robust Merchant Marine, outfitted with U.S. shipping vessels manned by American mariners, would be critical for addressing any potential logistical challenges associated with the transportation of supplies,” the letter states. The legislation has attracted support from maritime unions, commercial carriers, shipbuilding interests, and industry associations. The lawmakers also pointed to the Trump administration’s stated commitment to restoring U.S. maritime dominance. The latest letter demonstrates the breadth of congressional support for the initiative, with signatories spanning both parties and both chambers. Among those signing were Senators Susan Collins, Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Amy Klobuchar, Katie Britt, and John Fetterman, along with Representatives Joe Courtney, Rob Wittman, Salud Carbajal, and John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China. The letter was addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. While the House has already approved several SHIPS for America Act provisions, the final scope of maritime reforms included in the NDAA remains unresolved. The lawmakers are now pressing congressional leadership to preserve those provisions and go further before the defense bill reaches the president’s desk. “Now, we ask that these provisions be retained and strengthened in the final National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027,” the letter concludes. articles.body: C.H. Robinson reported revenue of $5.4 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 29.5% from the same period last year. The logistics company also recorded higher freight volumes and improved profitability across its main business divisions. Adjusted gross profit increased by 14.5% year over year. Meanwhile, adjusted diluted earnings per share rose by 28.6% to $1.80. The company reported diluted earnings per share of $1.67 under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). The Global Forwarding division generated revenue of approximately $1.15 billion, representing a 46.1% annual increase. Ocean shipments grew by 2%, while adjusted gross profit from ocean transportation increased by 23.2%. Global Forwarding also achieved an operating margin of 36.6%, an improvement of 660 basis points compared with the previous year. The results reflect the company’s efforts to improve efficiency across its international freight operations. Freight volumes and AI-driven productivity C.H. Robinson’s North American Surface Transportation (NAST) division recorded 3.5% growth in truckload and less-than-truckload volumes. In comparison, the Cass Freight Shipment Index declined by 0.3% during the same period. This marked the 14th consecutive quarter in which NAST’s annual volume growth exceeded the index. The division also reported a 17% increase in adjusted gross profit per truckload shipment. NAST achieved an operating margin of 40.3%, excluding restructuring costs. This represented an improvement of 110 basis points year over year. The company attributed part of its performance to its Lean AI strategy, which combines automation with operational improvements. According to C.H. Robinson, shipments handled per employee per day increased by more than 15% in NAST during the quarter. Productivity across both NAST and Global Forwarding has improved by more than 65% since the end of 2022. “Our industry-leading cost-to-serve model is highly scalable, and we expect it to strengthen further as we harness AI’s capabilities to automate more of the quote-to-cash lifecycle of a load,” said Dave Bozeman, CEO of C.H. Robinson. In October, the company also introduced new AI agents for ocean shipping, air freight and customs . The technology aims to automate complex freight forwarding tasks and improve customer responsiveness. C.H. Robinson is also preparing for its planned acquisition of RXO. The company expects to apply its existing operating model and AI technology to the integration process after the transaction closes. Bozeman said the acquisition would support the company’s broader growth strategy. However, C.H. Robinson continues to pursue organic growth alongside its planned expansion. The company returned $289.1 million to shareholders during the quarter through dividends and share repurchases.

articles.title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
articles.summary: Whatever the IMO decides in December, a broker will price a dry bulk trip the next morning. The vote changes which line of that fixture carries the carbon, and how much. Argyris Zafeiropoulos from Resilience & Compliance Advisory explains. Take a trip reported in the Baltic Exchange’s weekly round-up on 9 October: a...
articles.body: Contributions Dry Cargo Environment Regulatory The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture Splash October 30, 2026 0 315 3 minutes read Jack Hall / PA Media Assignments Jack Hall / PA Media Assignments Whatever the IMO decides in December, a broker will price a dry bulk trip the next morning. The vote changes which line of that fixture carries the carbon, and how much. Argyris Zafeiropoulos from Resilience & Compliance Advisory explains. Take a trip reported in the Baltic Exchange’s weekly round-up on 9 October: a 76,000 dwt Panamax, delivery East Coast South America, a transatlantic trip at $35,000 a day. Assume a grain cargo of 66,000 tonnes from Santos to Rotterdam, 12.5 knots and about 21 tonnes of fuel a day: some 26 days on hire and 400 tonnes burned. Priced today, the European bill on that trip is around €55,000 of EU allowances at about €88, the mid-October level, and €11,000 of FuelEU penalty: some €66,000 in total. That is €1.01 per tonne of cargo, roughly €2,600 a day, or 8% of the hire. Under a time charter the charterer normally pays both, through the BIMCO clauses, so it sits on top of the $35,000. Now the vote. MEPC 85 meets at the end of November, and the resumed extraordinary session on the Net-Zero Framework is pencilled in for 4 December. The framework was approved in April 2025 and its adoption adjourned for a year last October; it was debated again at MEPC 84 in the spring. Both outcomes remain possible. If it is not adopted Nothing changes on the morning after. The trip carries the same €66,000. The bill still grows, but on Europe’s timetable: when the FuelEU target tightens from 2% to 6% in 2030, the same trip costs about €85,000, or €1.29 a tonne, at today’s allowance price. There is a second effect on the other side of the ocean. The same ship on a fronthaul from Santos to Qingdao, twice the distance and twice the fuel, pays nothing in Europe, and would keep paying nothing. Between a Continent and a Far East discharge, one carries a carbon bill and the other does not. If it is adopted The framework prices fuel intensity, not location. From 2028 every tonne of fuel burned on international voyages counts, wherever the ship trades, against two targets: a ship pays $100 for each tonne of CO2-equivalent between the direct-compliance line and the base line, and $380 for each tonne above the base line. On the Rotterdam trip, assuming no change to the European rules, that adds roughly €29,000 in 2028, taking the carbon on the fixture to about €96,000, or €1.45 a tonne and 12% of the hire. By 2030 the two systems together come to about €136,000, some €2.06 a tonne and 16% of the hire. The largest change is on the Qingdao fronthaul. From zero, it would carry about €61,000 in 2028, close to what the Rotterdam trip pays in Europe today, and €106,000 in 2030. The carbon difference between the two discharge ranges narrows from €1.01 to about €0.52 a tonne in 2028. Three cautions belong with these numbers. The IMO charge is assessed per ship per year, not per voyage, so a trip’s share is an allocation. EU law requires the Commission to review the maritime ETS in the light of a global measure, so the two may not simply add up for long. And a ship that over-complies can sell surplus units, so the cost depends on the rest of the owner’s fleet. What changes on the desk For the broker, the practical point is less the price of a tonne of carbon than its allocation. If the framework is adopted, every fixture acquires a carbon line, not only those touching Europe, and the charter party has to say who carries it. On a time-charter trip, the BIMCO clauses written for the EU ETS and FuelEU do not by themselves cover an IMO remedial unit. A voyage charter leaves it with the owner, who will price it into the freight. The morning after the vote, the question at the desk will be the same one Europe has been asking since 2024: who pays the carbon on this fixture? If the framework is adopted, it will be asked on every route, not only those that touch Europe. articles.title: IMCA Launches 2030 Strategy to Guide Offshore Construction Industry
articles.summary: The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has launched IMCA 2030, a four-year strategy designed to ensure the association remains relevant, authoritative, and valuable to members as the offshore construction industry navigates…
articles.body: IMCA Launches 2030 Strategy to Guide Offshore Construction Industry Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Iain Grainger, Chief Executive Officer of IMCA. © IMCA The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has launched IMCA 2030, a four-year strategy designed to ensure the association remains relevant, authoritative, and valuable to members as the offshore construction industry navigates a period of significant change. Launched at the IMCA Global Summit in Antwerp, Belgium, the strategy responds to major industry trends including the growth of AI and automation, the energy transition, evolving regulatory requirements, and increasing competition for talent and skills. At the heart of the strategy are three strategic pillars: Advocating for technical excellence and standardization, Championing a safe, skilled, and diverse workforce, and Supporting sustainability and operational efficiency. These priorities will guide IMCA’s investment, services, and activities over the coming years. “The offshore construction industry is entering a period of profound change. New technologies, changing energy markets, and increasing regulatory demands are reshaping our sector, while competition for the next generation of skilled people continues to grow," explained Iain Grainger, CEO of IMCA. “IMCA 2030 is our response to these challenges and opportunities. It sets out a clear vision for how we will champion, protect, and support our industry and its workforce, ensuring it remains safe, sustainable, and fit for the future. The strategy reinforces our commitment to technical excellence, skills and competence, sustainability, and stronger advocacy, while ensuring we continue to deliver practical value for our members worldwide.” Under the strategy, IMCA will maintain its role as a global authority in diving, dynamic positioning, safety, and ROV operations, while building on its deep expertise in offshore survey and lifting and rigging, and supporting the industry to respond to evolving digital security threats. It will also strengthen its marine division through enhanced work on autonomy and remote operations, decarbonization, and offshore wind, alongside continued investment in eCMID, IMCA’s safety management system health check for offshore vessels. A major focus of IMCA 2030 will be supporting people and skills across the industry. Planned initiatives include a campaign to raise awareness of offshore careers, additional support for early-career professionals through IMCA’s Next Generation Network, and the creation of a joined-up competence management ecosystem to support the global offshore workforce’s continuing professional development. This will be supported by new initiatives such as digital logbooks and the IMCA Skills platform, providing on-demand access to training, professional development, and competence assurance. In addition, IMCA will enhance its policy and advocacy activities. Building on its longstanding involvement with the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the Association will increase its dialogue with the European Union and with national governments and regulators. It will focus on practical, coordinated regulation that improves safety, operational efficiency, decarbonization, and industry growth, while avoiding unnecessary complexity and cost. IMCA 2030 has been informed by member engagement and feedback. It sets out plans to increase regional participation and give Members more opportunities to contribute to technical guidance and the Association's direction, in part through a new Membership Committee that reports directly to the IMCA Board. Previously announced membership changes will take effect in January 2027, introducing a simpler more transparent framework designed to strengthen member engagement, improve members’ access to IMCA’s technical resources, and better support the evolving needs of the offshore energy industry. A new Associate category will open IMCA membership to independent consultants and sole traders, alongside academic institutions and research organizations undertaking commercial research.

articles.title: Port of Auckland welcomes new pilot vessel
articles.summary: Port of Auckland’s new pilot vessel Te Ihu has entered the Waitematā Harbour for the first time, completing a four-day sailing across the Tasman Sea after arriving into New Zealand via Opua in the Bay of Islands. A blessing ceremony was held with Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei at the port, marking the occasion alongside...
articles.body: Port of Auckland’s new pilot vessel Te Ihu has entered the Waitematā Harbour for the first time, completing a four-day sailing across the Tasman Sea after arriving into New Zealand via Opua in the Bay of Islands. A blessing ceremony was held with Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei at the port, marking the occasion alongside recognition of Pilot Boat Master Murray McGehan’s 50 years of service to the port. The vessel’s name was gifted by Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei, with Tumu Whakarae Lisa Davis explaining that Te Ihu draws on the knowledge and ingenuity of tūpuna. Traditional waka carvings beneath the prow, known as tauihu, were designed not purely decoratively but to work with the movement of water to support safe navigation, reflecting the vessel’s role in guiding larger ships safely into port. Davis described the naming as bringing together Murray McGehan’s lifetime of experience on the water and her own whakapapa connection to the Waitematā through Tuperiri and Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei, united by aroha for the harbour and its wellbeing. Chris Mills, Port of Auckland GM Marine, Multi-Cargo and Cruise, expressed delight at welcoming Te Ihu into the fleet after many months of preparation, acknowledging the contributions of Lisa Davis, Murray McGehan and Hart Marine in Australia to the vessel’s development. Te Ihu will undergo commissioning in the Waitematā Harbour before entering service in the coming months, with the existing Wakatere and Akarana pilot boats continuing to serve customers in the interim.
