(Photo: Contships Management) ATHENS/SOFIA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – A Greek container ship has sunk after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria on Wednesday, the Bulgarian government said, in the latest of a series of strikes in the western Black Sea this month that have raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine. The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET, loaded with 421 containers, was badly damaged by three sea drones as it passed through Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) – but outside its territorial waters – en route from Haifa in Israel to Constan?a in Romania. The crew of 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians were all rescued and transferred safely to the Bulgarian port of Varna, Contships Management said. Video footage verified by Reuters showed a sea drone driving alongside the vessel before turning towards its hull. In a separate video, an explosion was seen, causing the ship to eventually list. It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area. Ambrey, a global maritime risk management firm, has analyzed footage, reportedly filmed on a handheld device by a crew member on board, showing a matte black, 5-6 meter-long unmanned surface vehicle (USV) approaching the vessel at high speed. The USV was likely a variant of a Russian drone, said Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics, adding that its maneuvers indicated it was controlled remotely. “Ambrey assessed that the USV was likely a variant of, or derived from, the Russian Murena-300S design,” he told Reuters. At least six ships have been attacked by drones off Bulgaria this month, and about two dozen seafarers are feared dead, according to government statements. While it is not clear who has carried out the attacks, Bulgaria’s Prime Minister, Rumen Radev, has said that some of them appear to benefit Russia. Moscow has denied involvement in recent attacks and did not immediately comment on Wednesday’s incident. Andriy Ryzhenko, a former senior Ukrainian navy officer, said the drone visible in the video does not look similar to any model of Ukrainian naval drone that he is aware of. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought assistance to bolster security off its Black Sea coast. Bulgarian naval commander Kiril Mihaylov told national television authorities had been alerted to a possible drone attack by a French patrol aircraft, but had been unable to prevent it. The government said that initial inspections on Thursday had found no visible traces of pollution from the ship, whose cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids and industrial components. The company is expanding its fleet renewal program with an order for four additional LNG dual-fuel vessels and options for eight more. (Image: Wallenius Wilhelmsen) Wallenius Wilhelmsen is expanding its fleet renewal program with an order for four new dual-fuel car carriers and options for eight more, potentially adding 12 vessels in a deal valued at approximately $1.5 billion. The Norwegian shipping and logistics group announced Wednesday that it has reached an agreement with China’s Jinling Shipyard (Jiangsu) for the construction of four 9,900-car-equivalent-unit (CEU) pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs), with deliveries beginning in mid-2030. The agreement includes options for four additional vessels in 2031 and another four in 2032. If all options are exercised, total capital expenditure is expected to reach approximately $1.5 billion. The ships will be equipped with dual-fuel LNG engines and built to Wallenius Wilhelmsen’s Shaper Class design , which features hoistable decks, heavy-duty ramps and flexible cargo spaces capable of accommodating passenger vehicles, trucks and other rolling equipment. The latest order expands the company’s fleet renewal program to 26 vessels, including options, extending a newbuilding campaign launched in 2023 that Wallenius Wilhelmsen describes as the largest in its history. “We continue to see attractive opportunities in the segments we serve and want to ensure we have the capacity, flexibility and efficiency needed to support our customers well into the next decades,” said Xavier Leroi, chief operating officer of shipping services at Wallenius Wilhelmsen. “Expanding our newbuilding program with deliveries from 2030 reflects our confidence in the long-term fundamentals of the market,” he added. The newbuilding agreement follows a private placement completed earlier this month as the company continues investing in its long-term fleet requirements. Wallenius Wilhelmsen has already begun taking delivery of vessels under its existing Shaper Class program, with the new ships intended to modernize its fleet while providing additional capacity across its global shipping network. The company said the vessels’ flexible cargo configurations will allow it to respond to changing customer demand across the automotive and high-and-heavy equipment markets. The investment also reinforces the company’s shift toward alternative-fuel-capable vessels. LNG dual-fuel propulsion offers a pathway to reducing certain emissions compared with conventional marine fuels, although its overall climate benefits depend in part on methane emissions and fuel sourcing. Headquartered in Oslo, Wallenius Wilhelmsen operates approximately 130 vessels across 15 trade routes serving six continents. articles.summary: QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Image: Shutterstock/Oleksandr Kalinichenko DOHA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday. “In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we’re looking to have, you’d immediately see a spike in gas price and you’ll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn’t be generated,” Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan. Kaabi’s remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world’s largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The company signed a 20-year agreement on Thursday to buy 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) from Woodside’s US facilities. Last week it signed two agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa through 2054 from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants. Together, the deals amount to 7 mtpa in the past two weeks. “There’s more to come,” Kaabi said. Cheniere deliveries are not expected to begin until 2031. TRADING EDGE Kaabi, appointed CEO of the state energy giant in 2014, said the strategy was his idea and took shape about three months ago after QatarEnergy studied and ruled out pipeline options. “As we have seen, pipelines and pump stations or compression stations can be also targets.” The strategy builds on QatarEnergy’s LNG expertise, trading operation and shipping fleet. It requires no capital spending and is far cheaper than building pipelines or extra LNG trains, he said. “In normal circumstances you’d make a reasonable return and in critical circumstances — however that comes out and how long it is — you have actual proof today of what you could make.” QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March after several days of Iranian missile attacks on Qatar. It declared force majeure to affected buyers on March 4. Qatar accounts for around a fifth of global LNG exports, all of which pass through Hormuz. The company has extended force majeure until the end of 2026. Kaabi said being unable to ship volumes had taken a heavy toll on revenue. QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world’s largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world’s largest gas trading platform. “When you have the arbitrage capability that we have, the volume, number of ships, all the capabilities that we have, that’s why you can do it,” Kaabi said. The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG shipments pass. QatarEnergy can profit from the gap between lower US gas prices and higher European prices, Kaabi said. “You can imagine the arbitrage you can make, and that would make up some of the loss.” MORE DEALS TO COME Kaabi said he expects QatarEnergy to sign more 20- to 25-year supply agreements with US and other producers this year. The company’s target is “much higher” than 7 mtpa, though Kaabi declined to give a figure. He said QatarEnergy was in talks with “everybody,” including Venture Global, and would buy from whichever supplier offered the best commercial terms. Reuters reported last week that Venture Global is in advanced talks to supply 3 mtpa. Kaabi said QatarEnergy cannot offer US volumes to long-term customers as a backup to Hormuz disruptions because long-term customer contracts are point-to-point — requiring deliveries from specific export terminals to specific destinations. He added that customers had been understanding of the disruption. Iranian missile strikes on QatarEnergy’s main Ras Laffan gas processing facility in March damaged two of its 14 LNG trains, affecting combined capacity of 12.8 mtpa and knocking out about 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy said in March the damage would cost about $20 billion a year in lost revenue. Kaabi said on Thursday that repairs to the two trains would take about three years. The Pearl gas-to-liquids plant, a joint venture between QatarEnergy and Shell that was also damaged in the attack, should return to service by the first quarter of 2027, he said. He said Qatar could restart full LNG production within a week of a peace deal, provided ships were available. Output would be limited to about 83% of pre-war levels until the damaged trains return. Kaabi said no announced project had been canceled. Ras Laffan has capacity of 77 mtpa, and Qatar’s plan to expand LNG output to 142 mtpa remains unchanged, with all contracts awarded, he said. North Field East, South and West are all proceeding. The first North Field train is expected to start up in the first quarter of next year, although production would require a US-Iran peace deal to be in place. Kaabi said he had met Iran’s acting petroleum minister twice in recent weeks to explore oil and gas cooperation once the war ends. (Reporting by Andrew Mills in Doha and Maha El Dahan in Dubai. articles.summary: Nine maritime labor organizations say the Trump administration’s prolonged Jones Act waiver raises serious questions about compliance with federal law, including reporting requirements, immigration restrictions and the use of foreign...

Photo by Andy Randy Shutterstock Nine maritime labor organizations say the Trump administration’s prolonged Jones Act waiver raises serious questions about compliance with federal law, including reporting requirements, immigration restrictions and the use of foreign vessels in domestic commerce. Nine U.S. maritime labor organizations are raising fresh concerns over the Trump administration’s ongoing Jones Act waiver, warning that foreign-flagged vessels may be conducting domestic voyages without meeting federal reporting requirements and other legal safeguards intended to protect American mariners and national security. In an October 27 letter to House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) and Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee Ranking Member Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), the unions questioned whether the waiver complies with restrictions enacted under the Fiscal Year 2023 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The letter comes as the administration’s Jones Act waiver, first issued March 17 amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran, approaches its November 15 expiration following two extensions. The waiver allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport cargo between U.S. ports, temporarily setting aside the Jones Act’s requirement that domestic waterborne cargo move aboard U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed vessels. At issue is whether the waiver meets the NDAA’s requirement that such exemptions be granted only when “necessary in the interest of national defense to address an immediate adverse effect on military operations.” The unions argue that the extent of foreign-vessel activity under the waiver is difficult to reconcile with that standard. “The Administration, meanwhile, has provided Congress and the public with little of the required information regarding the need for the waivers and the availability of U.S. vessels as required by law,” the organizations wrote. They also allege that some waiver recipients have submitted inadequate documentation, missed mandatory reporting deadlines or failed to report their voyages altogether. Under federal requirements, vessel operators must submit post-voyage reports to the Maritime Administration within 10 days, including details about the vessel, cargo, ports visited and why the voyage served national defense interests. According to the unions, many operators have provided generic explanations or simply responded “not applicable” when asked to explain the national defense justification for their movements. Foreign Crews Raise Additional Legal Questions The labor organizations also raised concerns about the use of foreign mariners aboard vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce, including potential violations of immigration, employment and tax laws. The letter specifically questions whether foreign crewmembers holding D-1 visas are legally permitted to work aboard vessels transporting cargo between U.S. ports. “Immigration law, for example, prohibits foreign crewmembers holding a D-1 visa from engaging in domestic commerce, yet many waiver operations appear to employ precisely such D-1 visa mariners,” the unions wrote. The organizations also pointed to recent Internal Revenue Service guidance raising questions about U.S. tax obligations for foreign vessel operators and mariners participating in domestic transportation. They argue that allowing foreign crews to perform domestic shipping work without meeting comparable legal, licensing and security requirements puts American mariners at a competitive disadvantage. The letter further raises national security concerns, citing reported use of the waiver by Chinese state-owned shipping company COSCO and a separate instance involving Russian mariners. “These concerns are especially troubling because the Jones Act waiver authority was intended to strengthen national security,” the organizations wrote. “Instead, the program appears to have enabled hundreds of domestic voyages by foreign vessels crewed by foreign mariners operating under exemptions from laws that Congress never intended to set aside.” The unions cite media reports alleging espionage activity involving COSCO vessels near U.S. coastlines, but the letter does not establish that any vessel operating under the waiver engaged in espionage. Oversight Pressure Builds The latest letter adds to mounting congressional scrutiny of the waiver, including questions raised by Carbajal earlier this month over foreign-vessel reporting and compliance with federal law. As gCaptain reported on October 19, Carbajal asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to explain how the department is enforcing immigration, tax and maritime requirements aboard foreign vessels operating under the waiver. That inquiry followed gCaptain’s September reporting identifying evidence of at least 14 previously unreported domestic tanker voyages and a possible 15th, expanding on a Bloomberg Government investigation that found foreign vessels had transported more than $40 million in petroleum products without appearing in MARAD’s public waiver records. A gCaptain review of MARAD data published September 16 counted 255 completed movements under the original waiver and its first extension. The additional voyages suggested the official tally was incomplete. MARAD previously told Bloomberg Government that it lacks legal authority to compel operators to submit required reports. Jones Act enforcement falls to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The administration has since tightened its waiver procedures. Under rules introduced with the August 17 extension, operators must submit vessel availability requests before conducting a voyage, allowing MARAD to assess whether a qualified U.S.-flag vessel is available. The Department of War then determines whether the movement qualifies under the waiver. Whether those changes have addressed the broader compliance concerns remains an open question. Carbajal has requested a response from DHS by October 31. The October 27 letter was signed by leaders of nine maritime labor organizations, including the Seafarers International Union, American Maritime Officers, Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association, Masters, Mates and Pilots, Sailors’ Union of the Pacific, American Radio Association, Marine Firemen’s Union, AFL-CIO Maritime Trades Department and AFL-CIO Transportation Trades Department. “American mariners stand ready to support the nation’s energy, transportation, and national security needs,” the unions wrote. “We ask only for a faithful enforcement of the laws enacted by Congress.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. articles.summary: The US Department of Transportation has announced nearly US$500 million in funding for 35 port infrastructure projects across 19 states. articles.body: The US Department of Transportation has announced nearly US$500 million in funding for 35 port infrastructure projects across 19 states. The investment aims to modernise maritime facilities and strengthen cargo transportation networks. The US$498 million will be distributed through the Maritime Administration’s (MARAD) Port Infrastructure Development Program (PIDP). The programme supports improvements to coastal ports, inland waterways and Great Lakes facilities. Major port infrastructure investments The City of Whittier in Alaska will receive US$50.6 million to replace DeLong Dock and install a seasonal floating dock. The project also includes three pedestal cranes and additional marine equipment. Port Everglades in Florida has been allocated US$30.75 million to strengthen its liquid bulk terminal infrastructure. The project will also widen a vessel slip to accommodate larger ships and improve resilience during severe weather. In North Carolina, the State Ports Authority will receive US$11.25 million for improvements at Morehead City. These include heavy-lift cargo infrastructure, new crane rails and extensions to on-dock railway facilities. The project also involves optical character recognition (OCR) technology for cargo tracking. Meanwhile, Port Freeport in Texas will receive approximately US$9.4 million to replace an ageing bulk rice loader. The investment will also improve storage and berthing infrastructure. The Port of Corpus Christi Authority has secured US$7.15 million to develop digital twin capabilities. The project will incorporate LiDAR, sonar equipment, cameras and sensors to improve infrastructure monitoring. Additionally, the Red Wing Port Authority in Minnesota will receive US$10.16 million to modernise barge loading facilities. Rockport Harbor in Maine has been allocated US$698,750 for upgrades to commercial seafood handling infrastructure. US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said the investments aim to improve port infrastructure, strengthen supply chains and support employment across maritime communities. According to MARAD, the PIDP programme focuses on improving port efficiency and reducing transportation costs. It also supports infrastructure modernisation across the United States. The latest funding covers cargo-handling equipment, infrastructure resilience and digitalisation projects across different segments of the US port system.

articles.summary: Shell and TotalEnergies reported on Thursday sharply higher third-quarter profits and raised share buybacks, as war-driven energy prices and record refining margins helped both beat expectations.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Royal Dutch Shell LONDON, Oct 29 (Reuters) – Shell and TotalEnergies reported on Thursday sharply higher third-quarter profits and raised share buybacks, as war-driven energy prices and record refining margins helped both beat expectations. Shell raised its quarterly buyback to $5 billion from $3 billion, the second-largest buyback on record, while Total reiterated plans to buy back $2.5 billion of shares in the fourth quarter and said it would buy back another $2.5 billion in the first quarter of 2027. The shareholder distributions offer an insight into how oil majors plan to spend the profits generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is in its ninth month and has disrupted global energy supplies. Energy prices have driven inflation for customers globally and increased input costs for industry. Reflecting its higher payout, shares in Shell gained 3.2% in early trade on Thursday, while Total’s rose 1.8%, compared with a broader index of European energy companies rising 1.9%. BP, Chevron and ExxonMobil report results on Friday. Also on Thursday, Austria’s OMV reported its highest quarterly operating profit since 2022. Refining margins nearly quadrupled for both Shell and Total compared with a year ago. They reached $42 a barrel and $33.2 per barrel, respectively, helping to boost earnings to the highest since 2022, when Shell delivered a record $6 billion buyback program. Shell posted third-quarter net profit of $10.81 billion, above analysts’ average estimate of $10.33 billion and almost double the $5.43 billion it earned a year earlier. TotalEnergies reported adjusted net income of $9.1 billion for the July to September quarter, more than double the $4.0 billion a year earlier and above an expected $8.3 billion. Total’s refining and chemicals division posted record net income of $3.6 billion, more than five times the level of a year ago and double the previous quarter. CEO Patrick Pouyanné said a nearly 10% increase in refining throughput, along with strong oil trading, had captured historically high refining margins in Europe and worldwide. Total’s income in its LNG unit rose to $1.9 billion on average gas prices that were up 20% compared to the last quarter and strong LNG and gas trading. The company’s gearing fell to 9.1% at end-September from 13.1% at the end of the prior quarter, below its target of under 10% by the end of 2026. Jefferies called Total’s results “solid, not standout,” as hydrocarbon production reached 2.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, missing Total’s consensus by 4%, the broker said. Total also took a $1.9 billion impairment mainly tied to offshore wind and a South Korean petrochemical stake. Since December 30, 2022, Shell has delivered a 120% total shareholder return, including reinvested dividends, ahead of BP’s 78%, TotalEnergies’ TTEF.PA 84%, ExxonMobil’s 89% and Chevron’s 51%, according to Shell data. Shell beat expectations across all its segments. Its cash flow from operations, excluding working capital, rose to $21.7 billion from $12.24 billion a year earlier and beat expectations of $18.18 billion. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria said even with a roughly $5 billion buyback next quarter, Shell will likely miss its 40% to 50% payout ratio guidance for the year, a shortfall he attributed to abnormal macro conditions. Shell’s oil and gas output fell 17% in the first nine months of 2026 from a year earlier, mainly because war in the Middle East reduced volumes from Qatar. LNG liquefaction volumes rose 12%, driven by the ramp-up at LNG Canada and partly offset by the Qatari disruption. Shell halted production at its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar in March after an attack on Ras Laffan Industrial City damaged one of its two trains. It has has restarted the plant but at reduced output and says repairs could take about a year. Shell recorded $5.4 billion in non-cash increases to shipping leases, which count toward net debt. Shell booked an impairment of around $2 billion across its European biogas business, which includes assets from its 2023 $2 billion acquisition of Denmark-based Nature Energy, due to lowered expectations of growth in the market. Shell lowered its capital expenditure guidance for 2026 to $23 billion to $25 billion from $24 billion to $26 billion. articles.summary: Delays involving U.S.-built support vessels have pushed back turbine installation at Equinor’s Empire Wind offshore wind project off New York, with first power now expected in the first half of...

Image courtesy Equinor Delays involving U.S.-built support vessels have pushed back turbine installation at Equinor’s Empire Wind offshore wind project off New York, with first power now expected in the first half of 2027. Norwegian energy giant Equinor said Thursday that the 810-megawatt project is approximately 80% complete, but construction delays affecting specialized vessels needed to install its 54 wind turbines have pushed the schedule back several months. The update came as Equinor reported its third-quarter 2026 financial results. “Most of the remaining project scope relates to offshore turbine installation, which is expected to start next year,” Equinor Chief Financial Officer Torgrim Reitan told investors. “This is a bit later than planned.” The delay underscores the challenges of building out the U.S. offshore wind industry, particularly its reliance on specialized vessels and domestic shipbuilding capacity to meet requirements under the Jones Act. Empire Wind is using a turbine installation system developed by Maersk Offshore Wind, centered on the Singapore-built installation vessel Maersk Viridis . Because the vessel is foreign-built, it cannot transport turbine components between U.S. points under the Jones Act. Instead, the project relies on specially designed U.S.-built barges and tugs to deliver turbine components from the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal to the installation vessel offshore. The barges are designed to connect directly to Maersk Viridis , allowing turbine components to be transferred for installation without the installation vessel returning to port. While Maersk Viridis arrived off Pascagoula, Mississippi, in August for testing and preparations, delays involving the U.S.-built support vessels have pushed back the turbine installation campaign. Equinor said all 54 turbine foundations have been completed, along with the offshore substation and cable work. The project is located approximately 14 miles south of Long Island and is expected to generate enough electricity to power roughly 500,000 New York homes once operational. Despite the schedule setback, Equinor said it does not expect any change to the project’s total capital expenditure, although some spending will shift from 2026 into 2027. The company has previously estimated the project’s total investment, including redevelopment of the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal, at approximately $7.5 billion. Equinor also expects approximately $2.5 billion in U.S. investment tax credits, with roughly $2 billion expected to be recognized in 2027 and the remaining $500 million in 2028. The company said the revised construction schedule is not expected to affect the timing of those tax credits. The latest delay follows a turbulent period for Empire Wind, which has faced repeated attempts by the Trump administration to halt construction. The administration first ordered work stopped in April 2025, citing concerns over the project’s federal permitting process. That order was lifted the following month. A second suspension followed in December 2025, when the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management ordered construction halted on Empire Wind and four other offshore wind projects over national security concerns. Equinor challenged the suspension in federal court and secured preliminary relief allowing construction to continue. In its third-quarter financial statements, Equinor said the court dismissed the case on September 30, 2026, after the suspension order expired. The company said the dismissal eliminated the risk that a $2.7 billion project loan could become repayable within 12 months as a result of the order. Empire Wind remains one of the largest offshore wind projects under construction in the United States, with its latest setback highlighting the growing importance of domestic vessel construction to the industry’s ability to deliver projects on schedule. articles.title: QatarEnergy Purchases Long-Term LNG Supplies In Case of Future Hormuz Disruptions
articles.summary: QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida…
articles.body: QatarEnergy Purchases Long-Term LNG Supplies In Case of Future Hormuz Disruptions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 © MSM - stock.adobe.com QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday. "In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we're looking to have, you'd immediately see a spike in gas price and you'll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn't be generated," Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan. Kaabi's remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world's largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The company signed a 20-year agreement on Thursday to buy 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) from Woodside's US facilities. Last week it signed two agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa through 2054 from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants. Together, the deals amount to 7 mtpa in the past two weeks. "There's more to come," Kaabi said. Cheniere deliveries are not expected to begin until 2031. TRADING EDGE Kaabi, appointed CEO of the state energy giant in 2014, said the strategy was his idea and took shape about three months ago after QatarEnergy studied and ruled out pipeline options. "As we have seen, pipelines and pump stations or compression stations can be also targets." The strategy builds on QatarEnergy's LNG expertise, trading operation and shipping fleet. It requires no capital spending and is far cheaper than building pipelines or extra LNG trains, he said. "In normal circumstances you'd make a reasonable return and in critical circumstances — however that comes out and how long it is — you have actual proof today of what you could make." QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March after several days of Iranian missile attacks on Qatar. It declared force majeure to affected buyers on March 4. Qatar accounts for around a fifth of global LNG exports, all of which pass through Hormuz. The company has extended force majeure until the end of 2026. Kaabi said being unable to ship volumes had taken a heavy toll on revenue. QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world's largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world's largest gas trading platform. "When you have the arbitrage capability that we have, the volume, number of ships, all the capabilities that we have, that's why you can do it," Kaabi said. The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG shipments pass. QatarEnergy can profit from the gap between lower US gas prices and higher European prices, Kaabi said. "You can imagine the arbitrage you can make, and that would make up some of the loss." MORE DEALS TO COME Kaabi said he expects QatarEnergy to sign more 20- to 25-year supply agreements with US and other producers this year. The company's target is "much higher" than 7 mtpa, though Kaabi declined to give a figure. He said QatarEnergy was in talks with "everybody", including Venture Global, and would buy from whichever supplier offered the best commercial terms. Reuters reported last week that Venture Global is in advanced talksto supply 3 mtpa. Kaabi said QatarEnergy cannot offer US volumes to long-term customers as a backup to Hormuz disruptions because long-term customer contracts are point-to-point — requiring deliveries from specific export terminals to specific destinations. He added that customers had been understanding of the disruption. Iranian missile strikes on QatarEnergy's main Ras Laffan gas processing facility in March damaged two of its 14 LNG trains, affecting combined capacity of 12.8 mtpa and knocking out about 17% of Qatar's export capacity. QatarEnergy said in March the damage would cost about $20 billion a year in lost revenue. Kaabi said on Thursday that repairs to the two trains would take about three years. The Pearl gas-to-liquids plant, a joint venture between QatarEnergy and Shell that was also damaged in the attack, should return to service by the first quarter of 2027, he said. He said Qatar could restart full LNG production within a week of a peace deal, provided ships were available. Output would be limited to about 83% of pre-war levels until the damaged trains return. Kaabi said no announced project had been cancelled. Ras Laffan has capacity of 77 mtpa, and Qatar's plan to expand LNG output to 142 mtpa remains unchanged, with all contracts awarded, he said. North Field East, South and West are all proceeding. The first North Field train is expected to start up in the first quarter of next year, although production would require a US-Iran peace deal to be in place. Kaabi said he had met Iran's acting petroleum minister twice in recent weeks to explore oil and gas cooperation once the war ends. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Two California lawmakers are demanding that the Trump administration abandon reported plans to use ships for mass deportations, including the former Cal Poly Maritime Academy training vessel Golden Bear. Reps....

Join the leading maritime news network Photo Credit: Sophie Scopazzi Two California lawmakers are demanding that the Trump administration abandon reported plans to use ships for mass deportations, including the former Cal Poly Maritime Academy training vessel Golden Bear . Reps. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) and Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opposing the proposal, warning that deportations by sea would present major operational, safety and legal challenges while costing taxpayers millions of dollars. The letter follows an October 8 report by The New York Times that the administration was considering using ships to transport migrants to Central and South America. The discussions reportedly included the 500-foot Golden Bear , as well as ferries and potentially other vessels. The proposal remains preliminary, and no decision has been announced to use the Golden Bear or any other ship for deportations. “Mark my words, Donald Trump, Markwayne Mullin, and ICE will never use the Golden Bear for their mass deportation agenda,” Garamendi said in an October 28 statement. “Not only is deporting migrants by ship impractical, but it’s also deeply inhumane,” he added. The Golden Bear recently completed its final training voyage after 30 years of service at the California maritime academy. The vessel, originally built as the U.S. Navy oceanographic survey ship USNS Maury , has been used to provide hands-on training for generations of merchant marine officers. The ship is now being retired from academy service and returned to the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), making its potential availability for another federal mission a point of contention. Cal Poly Maritime Academy is awaiting its replacement training vessel, Golden State , part of MARAD’s National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program. According to the Times, the administration has also explored obtaining other vessels, including ships based in Europe, for possible deportation operations. The proposed voyages could take several days to reach destinations such as El Salvador, Honduras and Venezuela, compared with hours by air. They would also require substantial security personnel and arrangements for housing, feeding and supervising migrants throughout the passage. The lawmakers warned that those requirements could drive costs into the millions of dollars per voyage. Questions also remain about the legal authority to conduct such operations and the conditions under which migrants would be held aboard ships. Carbajal, the ranking Democrat on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee’s Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, warned that using vessels for immigration detention could create additional oversight problems. “ICE already operates without sufficient transparency or public accountability, and deploying maritime vessels as floating prisons will only open the door to potentially more abuses,” Carbajal said. The dispute also raises questions about diverting federal maritime assets and resources toward immigration enforcement. Garamendi argued that the administration’s previous use of military resources for deportation operations has already affected military readiness and warned that using ships could similarly strain U.S. sealift capabilities. Both lawmakers have previously challenged the administration’s use of military facilities, personnel and aircraft for immigration enforcement, including deportation flights from Travis Air Force Base in California. For now, there is no indication that the Golden Bear has been formally assigned to a deportation mission or that any maritime deportation operations have been authorized. But Garamendi pledged to use congressional oversight to prevent the ship from being used for that purpose. Speaking at a high-level debate of the Greek presidency of the UN Security Council on maritime security, Mitsotakis said commercial vessels must be able to navigate safely and freely even during times of conflict. "Targeted civilian commercial shipping is completely unacceptable. Commenting on a Turkey-Libya maritime accord which has drawn condemnation from Greece and Cyprus and three Arab states, Mitsotakis said that no bilateral arrangement could override international law of the sea, which provides a framework for cooperation and the peaceful settlement of maritime disputes. articles.title: Dockworkers Strike Against Arms Shipments at More Than 100 Ports Globally
articles.summary: Dockworkers in 22 countries will strike on Friday, protesting against war and the use of ports for arms exports in action organisers say could disrupt over 40% of Mediterranean cargo and snarl over $2 billion worth of freight.The strike, originally called by dockworkers' unions in Italy…
articles.body: Dockworkers Strike Against Arms Shipments at More Than 100 Ports Globally Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 © Adobe Stock/mangpink_s Dockworkers in 22 countries will strike on Friday, protesting against war and the use of ports for arms exports in action organisers say could disrupt over 40% of Mediterranean cargo and snarl over $2 billion worth of freight. The strike, originally called by dockworkers' unions in Italy, France, Greece, Spain's Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco, is now backed by more than 25 unions in 113 ports. The protest is expected to target major shipping hubs across Europe and beyond, including Hamburg, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras, Piraeus and Genoa, as well as Morocco's Tangier Med and India's Nhava Sheva. However, it was unclear how many dockworkers would take part or how severe any disruption would be. A spokesman for Italy's Genoa port said it expected only a limited impact, while Piraeus warned of disruption to ferry services for the Greek islands. Among the labour groups joining the protest are ver.di in Germany, Ireland's largest trade union SIPTU, 3F in Denmark and CGT Ports et Docks in France. Beyond Europe, the organisers said about a dozen ports in India could be disrupted, with the Water Transport Workers Federation of India (WTWFI) also supporting the action. The Global Sumud Flotilla, a pro-Palestinian campaign group that repeatedly tried to break Israel's blockade of Gaza to deliver humanitarian aid, said it would execute "coordinated, strategic actions on the water" to support the strike. Italian grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) called a 24-hour general strike in Italy for the same day, with protests scheduled in over 40 cities. Ferries will remain docked at Greek ports on Friday as Greek dockworkers, engineers and seafarers' unions join the strike. "We will send our own message of peace from Piraeus, and we will show our solidarity with the peoples suffering from war,” dockworkers at Greece's largest port, Piraeus, said in a statement, adding they would stop work from 0800 to 1100 GMT. Other unions in the country will stop working for 24 hours. https://reut.rs/4iINHqm 'WE WILL NOT WORK FOR WAR' In May 2026, dockworkers' unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones. Italian harbours, with Genoa at the forefront, have played a leading role in protests against arms shipments, frequently blocking cargo shipments bound for Israel and for US military bases. Over the 2021-2025 period, Europe became the world's biggest arms importer, data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute ‌showed earlier this year. "From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and genocide," unions said at a press conference announcing the strike. Representatives of India's WTWFI said that about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, with many more stranded at sea, highlighting the costs of armed conflicts on maritime workers. ($1 = 0.8925 euros) (Reuters)

articles.title: ABB Powers Third Hybrid Washington State Ferry Newbuild
articles.summary: ABB has received Notice to Proceed from Washington State Ferries (WSF), the largest ferry operator in the United States, to supply and integrate the power and propulsion system for third hybrid-electric newbuild ferry. This expands ABB’s involvement…
articles.body: ABB Powers Third Hybrid Washington State Ferry Newbuild Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 © ABB ABB has received Notice to Proceed from Washington State Ferries (WSF), the largest ferry operator in the United States, to supply and integrate the power and propulsion system for third hybrid-electric newbuild ferry. This expands ABB’s involvement in the program from two vessels to three and is part of WSF’s broader plan for up to 16 new hybrid electric ferries by 2040. As with the first two vessels, ABB will equip Vessel 3 with an integrated hybrid-electric power and propulsion solution centered on Onboard DC Grid and PEMS Power and Energy Management System. With Onboard DC Grid maximizing power distribution efficiency and energy storage integration, PEMS continuously manages available power sources to optimize energy use for vessel operating conditions. This reduces reliance on diesel engines, thereby helping to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. The 13.2-megawatt-hour energy storage system integrated by ABB is designed to enable all-electric, zero-emissions operations on short routes and in port. ABB’s scope of supply across the first three vessels also includes integrated marine automation, propulsion drives and motors, transformers, low-voltage systems, uninterruptible power supply systems, remote diagnostics, propulsion shafting, propellers, steering gear and rudders, in addition to engineering and commissioning support. Washington State Ferries burns approximately 19 million gallons of diesel annually. Its electrification program targets emission reductions of 76 percent in carbon dioxide, 75 percent in sulfur oxides, 94 percent in nitrous oxides, and 90 percent in particulate matter by 2040 – and ultimately envisions an emission-free fleet by 2050. The order further builds on ABB’s earlier involvement as the propulsion single source vendor in the WSF project, announced in 2024, with the contract amended to reflect the confirmed initial shipbuilding contract for two ships plus one option.

File photo: Cheniere Energy U.S. LNG giant raises full-year earnings outlook as Middle East supply disruptions boost demand for American exports Cheniere Energy, the largest U.S. exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG), reported a 15% increase in LNG cargo shipments during the third quarter as the war with Iran continues to disrupt Middle East energy supplies and reshape global gas trade flows. The Houston-based company reported Thursday that it exported 188 LNG cargoes during the three months ended September 30, up from 163 during the same period last year. Total export volumes increased 17% to 684 trillion British thermal units (TBtu). The increase comes as the conflict in the Persian Gulf has disrupted LNG exports from Qatar, one of the world’s largest suppliers, and raised concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruptions have increased demand for alternative supplies, including cargoes from the United States. Cheniere raised its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings guidance to between $8.75 billion and $9.25 billion, up from its previous forecast of $7.9 billion to $8.4 billion. Third-quarter revenue jumped 39% to $6.17 billion, while net income increased 12% to $1.17 billion. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) rose 18% to $1.9 billion. The results highlight the growing importance of U.S. Gulf Coast LNG export terminals as the Iran war continues to disrupt established energy shipping routes. Cheniere specifically highlighted a new agreement with QatarEnergy, the state-owned energy company behind Qatar’s massive LNG export industry. Cheniere said its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi operations signed long-term agreements in October to supply QatarEnergy with up to 4 million metric tons of LNG annually beginning in the early 2030s and continuing through 2054. One million tons of the contracted annual volume remains subject to a positive final investment decision on the first phase of Cheniere’s planned Sabine Pass expansion. The agreements are particularly notable given Qatar’s position as a major LNG producer and the ongoing disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with international markets. The contracts, which provide for delivery on a free-on-board basis, give QatarEnergy access to U.S.-produced LNG that can be marketed internationally without originating from the Persian Gulf. Cheniere also announced a separate 22-year agreement with Brazil’s Petrobras to supply 800,000 metric tons of LNG annually. The increased shipments follow the August completion of Cheniere’s Corpus Christi Stage 3 expansion in Texas, which added more than 20% to the company’s LNG production capacity. The project was completed ahead of its guaranteed completion schedule and within budget. “We achieved key milestones across the Cheniere platform in the third quarter of 2026, highlighted by the substantial completion of the seventh and final train of the CCL Stage 3 Project, the export of our 5,000th LNG cargo, and our continued commercial success in support of future brownfield growth at Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi,” said Jack Fusco, Cheniere’s Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer. Cheniere currently operates approximately 56 million metric tons per year of LNG liquefaction capacity across its Sabine Pass terminal in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Another 5 million tons of annual capacity is under construction, while more than 40 million tons is in various stages of regulatory permitting. The company is developing additional capacity at Sabine Pass and expects its two new Corpus Christi midscale trains to reach substantial completion in the second half of 2028. For the LNG shipping industry, the expansion of U.S. export capacity represents a growing source of cargo demand as global buyers seek alternatives to Middle East supplies. The company also reached a major shipping milestone in August, exporting its 5,000th LNG cargo from its U.S. Gulf Coast facilities. By October 23, Cheniere had loaded and exported approximately 5,120 cargoes totaling more than 350 million metric tons since beginning operations. During the first nine months of 2026 alone, Cheniere exported 559 LNG cargoes, compared with 485 during the same period last year. The figures underscore the growing role of U.S. LNG in international energy markets at a time when the war with Iran has exposed the vulnerability of traditional Persian Gulf export routes. articles.body: Tullow Oil Taps DeepOcean for Subsea Riser Job off Ghana Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 (Credit: DeepOcean) DeepOcean has secured a contract from Tullow Ghana to carry out subsea gas lift riser retermination work at the Jubilee field offshore Ghana, using its recently upgraded Orient Adventurer subsea construction vessel. The project involves a gas lift riser connecting the Kwame Nkrumah floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) vessel to the Jubilee subsea production system, with offshore operations scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026. DeepOcean's scope includes project management, engineering, riser disconnection, deck-side retermination, reconnection and pre-commissioning services. The company will deploy the Orient Adventurer, formerly known as Polar Onyx, for the offshore campaign, using its vertical lay system (VLS) to handle the riser operations. The Orient Adventurer recently returned to DeepOcean's fleet following a major upgrade and refurbishment program. The vessel is equipped with a 2,500-tonne under-deck carousel and a refurbished Huisman vertical lay system with 275-tonne top tension dynamic capacity, expanding DeepOcean's subsea construction and installation capabilities. “We have successfully deployed the Orient Adventurer on previous subsea construction projects in Ghana and are very familiar with the vessel's capabilities in the region. The vessel's VLS makes it particularly well suited for the safe and efficient deployment of the risers through the moonpool,” said Robin Mawhinney, Executive Vice President for DeepOcean’s EMEA region. The contract will be executed by DeepOcean Ghana Limited, a joint venture between DeepOcean and its local partner, with project teams in Accra, Ghana, and Sète, France, supported by engineering specialists in Aberdeen, UK. The Jubilee field is located approximately 60 kilometers offshore Ghana in water depths of around 1,100 meters. Production from the field is processed through the Kwame Nkrumah FPSO, which has a processing capacity of more than 120,000 barrels of oil per day and serves as the central hub for offshore production and associated gas handling operations.

articles.title: DNV Finds Aker BP, Höegh Evi's Offshore CO2 Injection Concept Feasible
articles.summary: DNV has issued a Statement of Feasibility for Aker BP and Höegh Evi's concept to transport liquefied carbon dioxide (CO2) by shuttle carriers and inject it directly into subsea wells for permanent storage at the Atlas project offshore Norway.The…
articles.body: DNV Finds Aker BP, Höegh Evi's Offshore CO2 Injection Concept Feasible Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 (Credit: Aker BP) DNV has issued a Statement of Feasibility for Aker BP and Höegh Evi's concept to transport liquefied carbon dioxide (CO2) by shuttle carriers and inject it directly into subsea wells for permanent storage at the Atlas project offshore Norway. The assessment covers the offshore infrastructure required to transfer CO2 from vessels into the reservoir, with DNV concluding that the main technical challenges and uncertainties identified are manageable at the current stage of development. The Atlas project, located on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), is designed to inject up to 6 million tonnes of CO2 annually in its initial phase, with potential for further expansion. The storage license has an estimated total capacity of 150 million tonnes, with first injection targeted for 2031 and operations expected to continue for more than 25 years. Under the preferred development concept, shuttle carriers operated by Höegh Evi would transport liquefied CO2 to the offshore storage site, where an offshore loading system and subsea lines would transfer it directly into injection wells. The approach would eliminate the need for new onshore facilities, cross-border pipelines and permanent offshore structures, while retaining pipeline transport as a future option. DNV's assessment was carried out using its technology qualification methodology under DNV-RP-A203 and DNV-SE-0160, identifying technical challenges requiring further design development and verification. “Direct injection from ship to reservoir requires the marine, subsea and injection systems to function as one integrated value chain. While further verification and maturation work will be needed as the project progresses, our assessment demonstrates that the concept is technically feasible and provides a sound basis for continued development,” said Prajeev Rasiah, Senior Vice-President & Regional Director for Northern Europe, Energy Systems at DNV. The latest milestone follows earlier DNV Approvals in Principle for Höegh Evi's liquefied CO2 carrier and floating CO2 reception and conditioning terminal (FCSO). Under the proposed transport system, captured CO2 from European industrial emitters would be delivered to a floating terminal for aggregation, purification and liquefaction before shipment to the offshore storage site. The terminal is designed to accommodate between 40,000 and 80,000 cubic meters of intermediate storage, while each shuttle carrier could transport up to 50,000 cubic meters per voyage. The floating terminal's conditioning operations were not included in the scope of the latest DNV feasibility assessment. Atlas Targets 2031 Start-Up The EXL011 Atlas license was awarded by the Norwegian Ministry of Energy in September 2024 and is operated by Aker BP with an 80% interest, alongside ORLEN with 20%. In October 2026, Aker BP and Höegh Evi were awarded $248.6 million (€223 million) from the EU Innovation Fund to support implementation of the Atlas cross-border CO2 transport and storage network, subject to a final investment decision (FID) in 2028. The project was also included in the European Commission's second Union list of Projects of Common Interest and Projects of Mutual Interest in April 2026. Subject to future investment decisions, Atlas is planned to begin operations in 2031. The marine-based direct-injection concept could also be applied at Aker BP's EXL005 Poseidon CO2 storage license on the NCS, where a similar subsea development approach is being evaluated.

The restrictions took effect this week, following a determination that Somalia was not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures at its ports. The decision, published in the US Federal Register, brings the number of countries on the Coast Guard’s affected-port list to 24. Under the established Port Security Advisory framework, ships that have visited an affected country among their previous five port calls face additional security and documentation requirements before entering the US. These include enhanced access controls, security records and reporting to the relevant Coast Guard captain of the port. Vessels may also be inspected for compliance, with deficiencies potentially resulting in delays or denial of entry. The new designation adds a compliance obligation for operators trading between East Africa and the US, including vessels calling at Somali ports before proceeding to other destinations. Somalia joins countries including Iran, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Venezuela on the list. The Coast Guard removed Nigeria from the advisory in August following a reassessment of its port security arrangements. The measure is separate from maritime warnings concerning piracy and attacks on shipping in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. articles.body: Cabling October 29, 2026 · 17 hours ago Seaway7 completes inter-array cable installation at East Anglia Three offshore wind farm 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Seaway7 Seaway7 has completed the final inter-array cable lay at the 1.4 GW East Anglia Three offshore wind farm in the UK. Seaway7's teams installed 95 inter-array cables, totalling more than 240 kilometers of cable loaded, laid and pulled into the foundations at the site. The achievement forms part of Seaway7’s wider scope on East Anglia Three, encompassing the foundations and inter-array cables for the project, and follows the completion of installation of all 95 monopile foundations and transition pieces earlier this year. With cable lay now complete, testing, termination and trenching activities continue as we progress the remaining work towards completion of Seaway7’s full project scope. The £4 billion (around €4.7 billion) East Anglia Three project, owned and developed by ScottishPower Renewables and Masdar, will comprise 95 Siemens Gamesa 14+ MW wind turbines and is the first UK offshore wind project to feature 115-meter blades. Wind turbine installation, which started in April, is also under way and is expected to be completed this year, with East Anglia Three scheduled to become fully operational by the end of 2026. articles.body: Gas Greater China Shipyards Jiahua Energy lines up $165m gas carrier at Jiangnan Adis Ajdin October 29, 2026 0 413 1 minute read Jiangnan Shipyard Jiangnan Shipyard Chinese chemicals group Jiahua Energy is stepping up its shipowning ambitions with plans to invest up to $165m in a 102,000 cu m liquefied hydrocarbon carrier at Jiangnan Shipyard. The Shanghai-listed company has secured board approval for the project, with Jiangnan Shipyard and China Shipbuilding Trading named as the counterparties. The vessel is scheduled for completion by June 30, 2030. The investment marks Jiahua’s second gas carrier project in just over two months and its first move into large ocean-going gas carriers. Jiahua intends to use the ship primarily to import ethylene for its PVC production operations, while retaining the flexibility to carry ethane. Any surplus capacity could be offered to Chinese petrochemical companies and traders. The company operates two PVC/VCM production units with a combined annual capacity of 600,000 tonnes and is looking to reduce its dependence on chartered tonnage and fluctuations in raw material freight costs. The newbuilding follows its August order for a 35,000 cu m liquefied hydrocarbon carrier at CIMC Sinopacific Offshore & Engineering, involving investment of up to CNY750m ($111m). That earlier vessel, scheduled for completion in 2029, is being developed through Jiahua’s shipping venture with its Meifu Port & Storage subsidiary and other investors. Jiahua’s latest project is to be funded through internal resources and other financing.
